summary:
The agent CLI on the host: its sandbox paths, robot-tool socket, environment and processes.

Codex and Claude Code run natively with their own logins and reach their model providers
directly. Each CLI's own sandbox confines the commands the agent runs: writes only in its
workspace, no internet, no host processes, and the repository, every session's private
files and the host's sockets unreadable. The session's frontend serves the robot tools on
a Unix socket; the CLI reaches it through mcp_bridge.py, the agent's Python through
RAX_MCP_SOCKET (auto_research_agent/api/runtime.py).

summary:
The dedicated Claude account for experiments: its setup-token and identity.

Experiments never use the operator's personal Claude login (~/.claude). A separate
account signs in once in its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and issues a long-lived
``claude setup-token`` token. The relay (messages_relay.Credential) reads only
that token file:

    ~/.config/rax/                  (0700; RAX_CLAUDE_EXPERIMENT_DIR overrides)
      claude-experiment-home/            dedicated CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, for sign-in only
      claude-experiment.token            the token (0600), re-read by the relay per request
      claude-experiment.json             identity (0600): email, organization, created_at

Every claude-login session's relay reads that one token file, so a rotated token applies to
running sessions at once.

Set up or rotate with ``bash scripts/setup_claude_experiment_login.sh``.

summary:
Host-only Anthropic Messages endpoint for Claude Code. Credentials never enter Docker.

Claude Code in the container talks to ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:17777,
which container_bridge.py forwards to this relay's Unix socket. The relay adds the
provider credential and enforces the same controls as the Codex Responses relay:
a model allowlist, a model-call count, local (client-executed) tools only, inline
media only, bounded bodies, and provider throttling retried before any byte reaches
the client. Token usage is appended to a host-side JSONL for the operator.

Providers:
- ``openrouter``: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/messages with the OpenRouter key.
- ``anthropic``: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with an API key (x-api-key).
- ``claude-login``: https://api.anthropic.com with the dedicated experiment account's
  long-lived ``claude setup-token`` token (harness/claude_cli/experiment_login.py),
  re-read for every request so a rotated token takes effect at once. The operator's
  personal Claude login (~/.claude) is refused.

summary:
Compact an auto-research conversation in its agent container (Codex or Claude Code).

One bounded, never-fatal agent invocation through the host model relay, with a stub
MCP endpoint that lists no tools, so nothing in the environment can change. It writes
the CLI's own compaction into the same transcript, which later resumes continue from.

- Codex 0.157 has no one-shot compact command; `exec resume` with
  model_auto_compact_token_limit=1000 forces its auto-compaction on that turn (a
  `compacted` record; user messages are kept, tool outputs summarized).
- Claude Code: `/compact <instructions>` on the resumed conversation (a
  `compact_boundary` record with pre/post token counts). If print mode does not run
  the built-in command, the auto-compact threshold is lowered for one turn instead.

summary:
Move a stopped auto-research session's simulators to another GPU before resuming it.

    bash scripts/move_session_gpus.sh --config runtime/auto-research/<run>/operator-input.json         --sim-gpu GPU-...

GPU placement is operator choice, not part of what a trial is. The session keeps it in three
copies (operator-input.json, configuration.json and the supervisor's state.json), which must
agree for `--resume`; this rewrites all three together and records the move in gpu-moves.jsonl.
Only the simulator has a GPU: the agent and its bundle containers have none. An agent-formal
copy listed on the old simulator GPU (formal_sim_gpus) moves with the simulator. Agent GPU
fields of sessions created before that (controller_gpu, training_gpu) are left as saved;
loading retires them. Refuses while any process still uses the session.

summary:
DexJoCo benchmark behind the shared harness: the official DexJoCo evaluation (unmodified)
exposed through the harness's simulator RPC. Host modules never import dexjoco or mujoco.

Reviews of finished DexJoCo exploration episodes from the simulator's ground truth.

Operator-side, stdlib + numpy only. When an episode ends the simulator writes
``sim/private_goal_report.json`` (services/dexjoco/session.py): success and termination, the
official environment's own info at reset and at the end (and which boolean info keys were ever
true, and the iPad's pressed digits), the official state with its privileged tail (each task
object's reset pose, services/dexjoco/objects.py), and the objects' poses and the points and
angles the success conditions use at reset and at the end, read from MuJoCo.

This module turns that into a short factual report: the outcome and why the episode ended (on
success, on a failure condition, at the step limit, or early by the agent or the harness), the
task's success and failure conditions as ``task_rules/<task>.md`` states them with what the
simulator measured for each, and how the task objects moved. One Gemini call explains it from
that report, the episode's tool trace and its final frames.

Agent-facing text carries relative measurements only (centimetres, degrees, counts): never
seeds, layout ids, world coordinates or the model's internal names. A standard review is the
analyst's explanation alone; a detailed review opens with the report and the analyst quotes
exact numbers. DexJoCo scores success or failure, so there is no partial score.

``TAIL``: the privileged tail of the official state vector (after the robot's 23 or 46
values), in the official config's ``proprio_keys`` order
(``DexJoCo/dexjoco/dexjoco/tasks/<task>/config.py``): each object's pose at reset (position in
metres, then a wxyz quaternion when it has 7 values), then the table height offset (1 value).
The environments fix these at reset, so the tail never holds final poses.

Live sources (``TAIL``'s third field and ``POINTS``): what the simulator reads at reset and at
the end of an episode, read-only from the environment's MuJoCo data by the official XML names:
``joint:`` a free joint's pose (its qpos, the same convention as the tail), ``body:`` a body's
world pose, ``site:``/``geom:`` a world position, ``sites:`` several sites' world positions in a
row, ``sensor:`` a sensor's value, ``hinge:`` a hinge joint's angle (rad). Every tail object with
a live source is read under its own label; the other labels are the points and angles a success
condition is defined on.

summary:
Host-side owner of the DexJoCo robot-only preview process (stdlib + msgpack + numpy only).

One persistent ``python -m services.dexjoco.preview_server`` per backend, started on the first
preview run on the simulator GPU and reused until the backend closes. It holds only the task's
official robot on a floor plane; it never sees a live episode.

DexJoCo robot-only motion preview service: ``python -m services.dexjoco.preview_server``.

Runs in runtime/envs/dexjoco. One persistent process per backend serves any number of preview
runs of one task's robot over the same msgpack RPC as the episode simulator.

Robot-only DexJoCo motion preview inside MuJoCo (runs in runtime/envs/dexjoco).

The task's own official robot (the Panda + Allegro MJCF that the task's official arena includes:
one arm, or the bimanual pair) stands alone on a floor plane, watched by fixed third-person
cameras. No arena, table, object, layout, seed or episode state is loaded or read.

Control is the official one. Each row is converted by the official code: the evaluation
wrapper's rotation-vector conversion (``DexJoCoOpenPIEnv._process_action``) and the policy
wrapper's split into the environment action (``SingleArmPolicyWrapper`` /
``DualArmPolicyWrapper``). The environment's step loop is then replayed, as in every official
``panda_*_env.py`` ``step()`` (e.g. ``panda_click_mouse_env.py`` lines 565-590,
``panda_bimanual_hanoi_env.py`` lines 613-645): ``n_substeps`` times [the official ``opspace()``
per arm -> arm torques, the hand joint targets -> the Allegro position actuators,
``mj_step``]. The keyword arguments of the ``opspace()`` calls (gains, damping, null-space
posture, gravity compensation) are read from the task env's own ``step()`` source rather than
copied; ``n_substeps``, the physics timestep and the home posture come from the env class
(``mujoco_gym_env.py`` lines 34-36, ``_PANDA_HOME``). Without objects the replay is the official
free-space dynamics; the environment's wall-clock pacing (``time.sleep``) is not replayed.

Start state. The official state vector has flange poses and hand joints but no arm joint
angles, so each run rebuilds its start: arm joints at the env's home posture (as ``reset()``
sets them), hand joints held at the start state's values, then the same per-step control drives
each flange from its home pose to the start pose: a ramp, then holds until the measured flange
is within ``SETTLE_POSITION_M`` / ``SETTLE_ROTATION_RAD`` of the start pose and the arm is
still. The official controller holds a pose with a small steady offset (about 0.3 mm and 6 mrad
were measured), so once the arm is nearly still the target is corrected by a fraction of the
remaining error each step until the measured pose, not the target, matches. The elbow
posture this yields follows the controller's null-space pull toward the home posture; after
motion the live arm's elbow sits differently (tenths of a radian per joint were seen), which
shifts the flange path slightly and matters near joint limits or elbow contact. The arm starts
at rest. The settle phase is reported (``settle``) and is not part of the frames.

summary:
Rotation and pose arithmetic for DexJoCo action rows: the ``dexjoco_rotation_math`` tool.

Pure computation: no episode, simulator or scene state. Safe to import in the host harness
interpreter; validation is plain Python and scipy loads on the first computation.

Rotation vectors and quaternions are converted with scipy's ``Rotation`` exactly as the official
evaluation wrapper converts rows (dexjoco_openpi_client/dexjoco_openpi_env.py): a row's rotation
vector becomes the environment's target quaternion with
``Rotation.from_rotvec(v).as_quat(scalar_first=True)`` (``_process_action``), and a measured
quaternion becomes a hold row's rotation vector with
``Rotation.from_quat(q, scalar_first=True).as_rotvec()`` (``stay``). Every reported
``quaternion_wxyz`` is the official conversion of the reported ``rotation_vector``.

A pose is a world-frame position (metres) and an orientation. ``compose_pose`` is pose_a followed
by pose_b expressed in pose_a's frame (world_T_b = world_T_a * a_T_b); ``relative_pose`` is
pose_b expressed in pose_a's frame (a_T_b = world_T_a^-1 * world_T_b).

summary:
DexJoCo simulator process: the official evaluation environment for one episode.

Runs only in ``runtime/envs/dexjoco`` (the official environment-dexjoco.yaml). The environment
is built at reset, when the layout's official seed is known (services/dexjoco/session.py).

One DexJoCo episode inside the simulator process (runs in runtime/envs/dexjoco).

The official evaluation wrapper ``DexJoCoOpenPIEnv`` (dexjoco_openpi_client) owns environment
creation, reset, stepping, the hold (``stay``), termination and success, exactly as
``dexjoco-openpi-eval`` drives it: ``_set_seed(seed)``, ``start()``, then one ``reset()`` per
episode, the click_mouse pre-roll, and policy rows through ``step()``. The only difference is
timing: the harness steps synchronously when the agent acts (zero-latency evaluation), while
the official loop holds with ``stay()`` during inference.

The session adds the harness contract: identity-checked RPC ops, agent observations (the
evaluation cameras at full resolution, optional depth rendered with the official
``collect_depth_frames``, calibration, the official state vector, the prompt), and the trusted
operator files that dashboards and formal scoring read. Privileged state (object poses,
the layout) stays in operator-only files.

Episode reviews: an operator-side analyst's review of each finished exploration episode.

The lifecycle is shared by every benchmark whose simulator writes ground truth
(``services.benchmarks``: ``episode_reviews``):

- ``runner``: settings (off, on, detailed) in ``<session>/operator-analysis/settings.json``,
  background workers that wait for a closed episode's simulator files, the Gemini call through
  the OpenRouter router, the cost ledger, the 0600 operator record and the agent's

- ``common``: helpers every benchmark's analysis uses (condensed tool trace, final RGB frames,
  the Gemini call, the budget).

A benchmark supplies its ground truth and wording through its adapter hook
``review_analysis()``, a module with:

- ``ground_truth_report(sim_dir)``: the report of one finished episode (a dict whose
  ``episode_id`` and ``episode_mode`` name it), or None when the simulator wrote nothing;
- ``condensed_trace(mcp_trace)``: one line per tool call;
- ``explain(router, report, trace, images, *, task_instruction, detailed, score)``:
  the analyst's explanation and its cost, ``(text, cost_usd)``;
- ``agent_review(report, explanation, *, episode_number, detailed, score, run)``: the
  agent-safe Markdown of ``review.md``;
- ``task_instruction(task)``: the task's instruction for the analyst.

summary:
Jinja rendering of trusted workspace sources.

Sources are markdown with Jinja statements on their own lines, e.g.

    {% if camera_geometry %}
    ...text for depth-capable profiles...
    {% else %}
    ...RGB-only text...
    {% endif %}

trim_blocks/lstrip_blocks drop the statement lines entirely, so rendered text keeps
the source's line layout. Unknown names fail the build (StrictUndefined).

Reusable passages are registered blocks (agent_blocks/blocks.toml) inserted with
{{ block("<id>") }} on a line of its own; the setup's facts, the recipe's `vocab`
and any keyword parameters are available inside a block. Every block a file uses
is recorded, so a build can report which blocks produced each file.

summary:

Codex and Claude Code run natively with their own logins and reach their model providers
directly. Each CLI's own sandbox confines the commands the agent runs: writes only in its
workspace, no internet, no host processes, and the repository, every session's private
files and the host's sockets unreadable. The session's frontend serves the robot tools on
a Unix socket; the CLI reaches it through mcp_bridge.py, the agent's Python through
RAX_MCP_SOCKET (auto_research_agent/api/runtime.py).

summary:
The dedicated Claude account for experiments: its setup-token and identity.

Experiments never use the operator's personal Claude login (~/.claude). A separate
account signs in once in its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and issues a long-lived
``claude setup-token`` token. Sessions sign Claude Code in with only that token
(login.Credential):

    ~/.config/rax/                  (0700; RAX_CLAUDE_EXPERIMENT_DIR overrides)
      claude-experiment-home/            dedicated CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, for sign-in only
      claude-experiment.token            the token (0600), read at each launch
      claude-experiment.json             identity (0600): email, organization, created_at

Every claude-login launch and resume reads that one token file, so a rotated token applies
from a session's next launch.

Set up or rotate with ``bash scripts/setup_claude_experiment_login.sh``.

summary:

One bounded, never-fatal native agent invocation with a stub MCP endpoint that lists no
tools, so nothing in the environment can change. It writes the CLI's own compaction into
the same transcript, which later resumes continue from.

  model_auto_compact_token_limit=1000 forces its auto-compaction on that turn (a
  `compacted` record; user messages are kept, tool outputs summarized).
- Claude Code: `/compact <instructions>` on the resumed conversation (a
  `compact_boundary` record with pre/post token counts). If print mode does not run
  the built-in command, the auto-compact threshold is lowered for one turn instead.

summary:

    bash scripts/move_session_gpus.sh --config runtime/auto-research/<run>/operator-input.json         --sim-gpu GPU-...

GPU placement is operator choice, not part of what a trial is. The session keeps it in three
copies (operator-input.json, configuration.json and the supervisor's state.json), which must
agree for `--resume`; this rewrites all three together and records the move in gpu-moves.jsonl.

of sessions created before that (controller_gpu, training_gpu) are left as saved; loading
retires them. Refuses while any process still uses the session.

summary:
DexJoCo benchmark behind the shared harness: the official DexJoCo evaluation (unmodified)
exposed through the harness's simulator RPC. Host modules never import dexjoco or mujoco.

Reviews of finished DexJoCo exploration episodes from the simulator's ground truth.

Operator-side, stdlib + numpy only. When an episode ends the simulator writes
``sim/private_goal_report.json`` (services/dexjoco/session.py): success and termination, the
official environment's own info at reset and at the end (and which boolean info keys were ever
true, and the iPad's pressed digits), the official state with its privileged tail (each task
object's reset pose, services/dexjoco/objects.py), and the objects' poses and the points and
angles the success conditions use at reset and at the end, read from MuJoCo.

This module turns that into a short factual report: the outcome and why the episode ended (on
success, on a failure condition, at the step limit, or early by the agent or the harness), the
task's success and failure conditions as ``task_rules/<task>.md`` states them with what the
simulator measured for each, and how the task objects moved. One Gemini call explains it from
that report, the episode's tool trace and its final frames.

Agent-facing text carries relative measurements only (centimetres, degrees, counts): never
seeds, layout ids, world coordinates or the model's internal names. A standard review is the
analyst's explanation alone; a detailed review opens with the report and the analyst quotes
exact numbers. DexJoCo scores success or failure, so there is no partial score.

``TAIL``: the privileged tail of the official state vector (after the robot's 23 or 46
values), in the official config's ``proprio_keys`` order
(``DexJoCo/dexjoco/dexjoco/tasks/<task>/config.py``): each object's pose at reset (position in
metres, then a wxyz quaternion when it has 7 values), then the table height offset (1 value).
The environments fix these at reset, so the tail never holds final poses.

Live sources (``TAIL``'s third field and ``POINTS``): what the simulator reads at reset and at
the end of an episode, read-only from the environment's MuJoCo data by the official XML names:
``joint:`` a free joint's pose (its qpos, the same convention as the tail), ``body:`` a body's
world pose, ``site:``/``geom:`` a world position, ``sites:`` several sites' world positions in a
row, ``sensor:`` a sensor's value, ``hinge:`` a hinge joint's angle (rad). Every tail object with
a live source is read under its own label; the other labels are the points and angles a success
condition is defined on.

summary:
Host-side owner of the DexJoCo robot-only preview process (stdlib + msgpack + numpy only).

One persistent ``python -m services.dexjoco.preview_server`` per backend, started on the first
preview run on the simulator GPU and reused until the backend closes. It holds only the task's
official robot on a floor plane; it never sees a live episode.

DexJoCo robot-only motion preview service: ``python -m services.dexjoco.preview_server``.

Runs in runtime/envs/dexjoco. One persistent process per backend serves any number of preview
runs of one task's robot over the same msgpack RPC as the episode simulator.

Robot-only DexJoCo motion preview inside MuJoCo (runs in runtime/envs/dexjoco).

The task's own official robot (the Panda + Allegro MJCF that the task's official arena includes:
one arm, or the bimanual pair) stands alone on a floor plane, watched by fixed third-person
cameras. No arena, table, object, layout, seed or episode state is loaded or read.

Control is the official one. Each row is converted by the official code: the evaluation
wrapper's rotation-vector conversion (``DexJoCoOpenPIEnv._process_action``) and the policy
wrapper's split into the environment action (``SingleArmPolicyWrapper`` /
``DualArmPolicyWrapper``). The environment's step loop is then replayed, as in every official
``panda_*_env.py`` ``step()`` (e.g. ``panda_click_mouse_env.py`` lines 565-590,
``panda_bimanual_hanoi_env.py`` lines 613-645): ``n_substeps`` times [the official ``opspace()``
per arm -> arm torques, the hand joint targets -> the Allegro position actuators,
``mj_step``]. The keyword arguments of the ``opspace()`` calls (gains, damping, null-space
posture, gravity compensation) are read from the task env's own ``step()`` source rather than
copied; ``n_substeps``, the physics timestep and the home posture come from the env class
(``mujoco_gym_env.py`` lines 34-36, ``_PANDA_HOME``). Without objects the replay is the official
free-space dynamics; the environment's wall-clock pacing (``time.sleep``) is not replayed.

Start state. The official state vector has flange poses and hand joints but no arm joint
angles, so each run rebuilds its start: arm joints at the env's home posture (as ``reset()``
sets them), hand joints held at the start state's values, then the same per-step control drives
each flange from its home pose to the start pose: a ramp, then holds until the measured flange
is within ``SETTLE_POSITION_M`` / ``SETTLE_ROTATION_RAD`` of the start pose and the arm is
still. The official controller holds a pose with a small steady offset (about 0.3 mm and 6 mrad
were measured), so once the arm is nearly still the target is corrected by a fraction of the
remaining error each step until the measured pose, not the target, matches. The elbow
posture this yields follows the controller's null-space pull toward the home posture; after
motion the live arm's elbow sits differently (tenths of a radian per joint were seen), which
shifts the flange path slightly and matters near joint limits or elbow contact. The arm starts
at rest. The settle phase is reported (``settle``) and is not part of the frames.

summary:
Rotation and pose arithmetic for DexJoCo action rows: the ``dexjoco_rotation_math`` tool.

Pure computation: no episode, simulator or scene state. Safe to import in the host harness
interpreter; validation is plain Python and scipy loads on the first computation.

Rotation vectors and quaternions are converted with scipy's ``Rotation`` exactly as the official
evaluation wrapper converts rows (dexjoco_openpi_client/dexjoco_openpi_env.py): a row's rotation
vector becomes the environment's target quaternion with
``Rotation.from_rotvec(v).as_quat(scalar_first=True)`` (``_process_action``), and a measured
quaternion becomes a hold row's rotation vector with
``Rotation.from_quat(q, scalar_first=True).as_rotvec()`` (``stay``). Every reported
``quaternion_wxyz`` is the official conversion of the reported ``rotation_vector``.

A pose is a world-frame position (metres) and an orientation. ``compose_pose`` is pose_a followed
by pose_b expressed in pose_a's frame (world_T_b = world_T_a * a_T_b); ``relative_pose`` is
pose_b expressed in pose_a's frame (a_T_b = world_T_a^-1 * world_T_b).

symbols.name: validate
symbols.doc: Complete validation before computation; raises RejectedBeforeAction.

symbols.name: _nearest
symbols.doc:
The rotation vector of the same rotation closest to ``near``: angle t about n equals
angle t - 2 pi about n, so consecutive rows need not jump across the pi boundary.

summary:
DexJoCo simulator process: the official evaluation environment for one episode.

Runs only in ``runtime/envs/dexjoco`` (the official environment-dexjoco.yaml). The environment
is built at reset, when the layout's official seed is known (services/dexjoco/session.py).

One DexJoCo episode inside the simulator process (runs in runtime/envs/dexjoco).

The official evaluation wrapper ``DexJoCoOpenPIEnv`` (dexjoco_openpi_client) owns environment
creation, reset, stepping, the hold (``stay``), termination and success, exactly as
``dexjoco-openpi-eval`` drives it: ``_set_seed(seed)``, ``start()``, then one ``reset()`` per
episode, the click_mouse pre-roll, and policy rows through ``step()``. The only difference is
timing: the harness steps synchronously when the agent acts (zero-latency evaluation), while
the official loop holds with ``stay()`` during inference.

The session adds the harness contract: identity-checked RPC ops, agent observations (the
evaluation cameras at full resolution, optional depth rendered with the official
``collect_depth_frames``, calibration, the official state vector, the prompt), and the trusted
operator files that dashboards and formal scoring read. Privileged state (object poses,
the layout) stays in operator-only files.

The official wrapper discards ``info`` and slices the state; the operator files need the
environment's own success info and the privileged state tail. Since the last reset it also
remembers which boolean info keys were ever true (e.g. ``hammer_hit``, ``shutter_pressed``)
and the entries of list-valued ones (``pressed_digits``), for episode reviews. Behaviour is
unchanged.

summary: Usage projected by native DSH steps, including cached prompt tokens and retries.

Episode reviews: an operator-side analyst's review of each finished exploration episode.

The lifecycle is shared by every benchmark whose simulator writes ground truth
(``services.benchmarks``: ``episode_reviews``):

- ``runner``: settings (off, on, detailed) in ``<session>/operator-analysis/settings.json``,
  background workers that wait for a closed episode's simulator files, the Gemini call through
  the OpenRouter router, the cost ledger, the 0600 operator record and the agent's
  ``review.md`` in that episode's published run directory. Formal episodes are never reviewed.
- ``common``: helpers every benchmark's analysis uses (condensed tool trace, final RGB frames,
  the Gemini call, the budget).
- ``workspace``: the TASK.md "Episode reviews" section and the AGENTS.md reminder.

A benchmark supplies its ground truth and wording through its adapter hook
``review_analysis()``, a module with:

- ``ground_truth_report(sim_dir)``: the report of one finished episode (a dict whose
  ``episode_id`` and ``episode_mode`` name it), or None when the simulator wrote nothing;
- ``condensed_trace(mcp_trace)``: one line per tool call;
- ``explain(router, report, trace, images, *, task_instruction, detailed, score)``:
  the analyst's explanation and its cost, ``(text, cost_usd)``;
- ``agent_review(report, explanation, *, episode_number, detailed, score, run)``: the
  agent-safe Markdown of ``review.md``;
- ``task_instruction(task)``: the task's instruction for the analyst.

Background reviews of finished exploration episodes (operator-side), for every benchmark whose
simulator writes ground truth.

Reviews are part of closing an episode: the session's episode management (the supervisor
for single-environment episodes and rehearsals, the exploration pool for parallel ones)
reports each closed episode to the session's ``EpisodeReviews``, owned by its MCP service
(``services.controller.frontend``), so no dashboard is involved. While the operator has
reviews on, every closed exploration or rehearsal episode gets one review from the
session's benchmark's analysis (its adapter's ``review_analysis()``, see
``services/episode_reviews/__init__.py``):
- the operator record: ``<session>/operator-analysis/<episode_id>.json`` (0600), never
  readable by the agent;
- the agent's copy: ``review.md`` in that episode's own published run directory (the
  ``artifacts.directory`` its ``finish`` or ``rehearse`` reply named), which the agent reads
  read-only under ``runtime/autonomous_controller/runs/`` in its workspace. TASK.md says where.

Formal episodes are never reviewed. Gemini costs go to ``operator-analysis/usage.jsonl``
and never to the agent's own budget.

One durable episode ledger, independent workers, serialized control per slot.

The ledger counts starts (including initial starts and failed startups), not tool
calls. A reset reserves a new seed before replacing the old episode. Exhaustion
never closes another slot's live episode. No agent can select seeds or create slots.

summary:
Model of the robot you control: Unitree G1 (29 body joints) with two Dex3 hands.

Everything here comes from ``robot.json`` next to this file, which was exported from the
simulated robot itself (its USD articulation) and checked against the simulator's measured
link poses. Pure Python 3.6+; NumPy and Pillow are used when present.

An observation is the JSON of an observe or motion reply (its first text block), saved to a
file; a saved frame-sequence manifest works too (its last frame is used). Quick start::

    S=.agents/skills/robot-interface/scripts
    python3 $S/g1_model.py pose --observation obs.json             # key points, level frame
    python3 $S/g1_model.py pose --observation obs.json --png /tmp/pose.png   # stick figure
    python3 $S/g1_model.py deproject 320 300 --observation obs.json --depth-png frame_depth.png
    python3 $S/g1_model.py project 0.45 -0.2 -0.1 --observation obs.json   # level frame -> pixel
    python3 $S/g1_model.py semantic40      # what every action dimension controls
    python3 $S/g1_model.py hand            # Dex3 joints, open/closed poses, fingertips

From Python::

    import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "/workspace/.agents/skills/robot-interface/scripts")
    import g1_model as g1
    pose = g1.pose_from_observation(g1.load_observation("obs.json"))   # or g1.MODEL.fk(joints29, ...)
    pose.point("right_hand_center", frame="level")            # metres, wxyz
    pose.deproject(u, v, depth_m, frame="level")               # depth = distance to image plane

Frames (all metres, quaternions [w, x, y, z]):

- ``pelvis``: the robot root body (the observation's root orientation is this body's
  orientation). x forward, y left, z up.
- ``level``: same origin as ``pelvis``, but gravity-aligned: z points straight up and x is the
  pelvis forward direction projected onto the horizontal plane. Needs the root orientation;
  without it ``level`` equals ``pelvis``. Heights in ``level`` are relative to the pelvis origin.
- any link name, ``camera`` (``d435_link``: x along the optical axis, y left, z up) and
  ``camera_optical`` (x right, y down, z forward: the image/depth frame).

There is no world frame: nothing here knows where the robot or any object is in the room.

summary:
The agent CLI on the host: its sandbox paths, robot-tool socket, environment and processes.

Codex and Claude Code run natively with their own logins and reach their model providers
directly. Each CLI's own sandbox confines the commands the agent runs: writes only in its
workspace, no internet, no host processes, and the repository, every session's private
files and the host's sockets unreadable. The session's frontend serves the robot tools on
a Unix socket; the CLI reaches it through mcp_bridge.py, the agent's Python through
RAX_MCP_SOCKET (auto_research_agent/api/runtime.py).

summary:
The dedicated Claude account for experiments: its setup-token and identity.

Experiments never use the operator's personal Claude login (~/.claude). A separate
account signs in once in its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and issues a long-lived
``claude setup-token`` token. The relay (messages_relay.Credential) reads only
that token file:

    ~/.config/rax/                  (0700; RAX_CLAUDE_EXPERIMENT_DIR overrides)
      claude-experiment-home/            dedicated CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, for sign-in only
      claude-experiment.token            the token (0600), re-read by the relay per request
      claude-experiment.json             identity (0600): email, organization, created_at

Every claude-login session's relay reads that one token file, so a rotated token applies to
running sessions at once.

Set up or rotate with ``bash scripts/setup_claude_experiment_login.sh``.

summary:
Host-only Anthropic Messages endpoint for Claude Code. Credentials never enter Docker.

Claude Code in the container talks to ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:17777,
which container_bridge.py forwards to this relay's Unix socket. The relay adds the
provider credential and enforces the same controls as the Codex Responses relay:
a model allowlist, a model-call count, local (client-executed) tools only, inline
media only, bounded bodies, and provider throttling retried before any byte reaches
the client. Token usage is appended to a host-side JSONL for the operator.

Providers:
- ``openrouter``: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/messages with the OpenRouter key.
- ``anthropic``: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with an API key (x-api-key).
- ``claude-login``: https://api.anthropic.com with the dedicated experiment account's
  long-lived ``claude setup-token`` token (harness/claude_cli/experiment_login.py),
  re-read for every request so a rotated token takes effect at once. The operator's
  personal Claude login (~/.claude) is refused.

summary:
Compact an auto-research conversation in its agent container (Codex or Claude Code).

One bounded, never-fatal agent invocation through the host model relay, with a stub
MCP endpoint that lists no tools, so nothing in the environment can change. It writes
the CLI's own compaction into the same transcript, which later resumes continue from.

- Codex 0.157 has no one-shot compact command; `exec resume` with
  model_auto_compact_token_limit=1000 forces its auto-compaction on that turn (a
  `compacted` record; user messages are kept, tool outputs summarized).
- Claude Code: `/compact <instructions>` on the resumed conversation (a
  `compact_boundary` record with pre/post token counts). If print mode does not run
  the built-in command, the auto-compact threshold is lowered for one turn instead.

summary:
Move a stopped auto-research session's simulators to another GPU before resuming it.

    bash scripts/move_session_gpus.sh --config runtime/auto-research/<run>/operator-input.json         --sim-gpu GPU-...

GPU placement is operator choice, not part of what a trial is. The session keeps it in three
copies (operator-input.json, configuration.json and the supervisor's state.json), which must
agree for `--resume`; this rewrites all three together and records the move in gpu-moves.jsonl.
Only the simulator has a GPU: the agent and its bundle containers have none. An agent-formal
copy listed on the old simulator GPU (formal_sim_gpus) moves with the simulator. Agent GPU
fields of sessions created before that (controller_gpu, training_gpu) are left as saved;
loading retires them. Refuses while any process still uses the session.

Each task's three episodes (services/humanoid/expert_sources.json: the first three lexicographic
episodes of the raw SONIC branch) are downloaded from ModelScope at the revision pinned in
dependencies.lock and checked against their pinned size and sha256. Their NPZ and front-camera video
are kept unchanged; beside them each episode gets a per-frame JSON view (`trajectory.jsonl`, with the
SONIC virtual points derived from the measured joints by forward kinematics of the released G1
MuJoCo description), a byte-offset index, metadata, a catalog of the raw arrays and uniformly spaced
front-camera previews. The set is installed at ``runtime/reference-demos/humanoid/<task>/experts/``
with a manifest of every file's sha256. Nothing recorded is executed. Needs NumPy and OpenCV (the host
environment) and a few GB of free space per task.

``--images`` derives each task's camera-only set from its installed episodes, for sessions with
``expert_content: images``: ``runtime/reference-demos/humanoid/<task>/expert-images/`` holds, per
episode, the front-camera video, the previews and the depth of every frame, and nothing of the
commanded references, measured motion, object states or layout.

symbols.name: resume_agent_formal
symbols.doc:
Finish an agent formal that was stopped before every layout had an outcome.

Episodes with an outcome stand. A stopped (interrupted) episode has none: its copy never
finished and it was never scored, so a fresh copy of the same frozen checkpoint plays that
layout from the start. The stopped attempt moves from the results to the batch's
interruptions record and its worker folder moves aside, so every reader of the results and
worker folders sees one episode per layout.

symbols.name: _worker_result
symbols.doc:
The worker's own episode record is authoritative.

A worker that started its episode but never finalized it counts as an error,
like a sequential timeout. One that never started an episode is a systemic
failure (spawn, preflight, bundle import), which interrupts the batch exactly
as it would in the sequential loop. A later nonzero worker exit is
recorded separately and cannot invalidate finalized task evidence.

symbols.name: _recover_parallel_formal
symbols.doc: After a supervisor crash: stop this session's workers and keep their evidence.

symbols.name: _run_parallel_formal

summary:

Body-frame only. Every pose is expressed in the ``pelvis`` frame (the articulation root,
default) or in the ``torso_link`` frame (``frame="torso"``), evaluated at the joint
configuration you pass. Metres, radians, quaternions ``[w, x, y, z]``. Joint names are the
simulator's canonical names (:data:`CANONICAL29`).

Quick reference::

    from services.humanoid import g1
    fk = g1.forward_kinematics(joints)                 # named frame poses, CPU only
    table = {"cuboid": {"dims": [0.5, 1.2, 0.04], "pose_wxyz": [0.55, 0, -0.02, 1, 0, 0, 0]}}
    ik = g1.solve_arm_ik("right", [0.35, -0.2, 0.08], [0.7071068, -0.7071068, 0, 0],
                         current_joints=joints, end_effector="hand_center", obstacles=[table])
    plan = g1.plan_arm_motion("right", [0.35, -0.2, 0.08], [0.7071068, -0.7071068, 0, 0],
                              current_joints=joints, end_effector="hand_center", obstacles=[table])

CUDA is only initialised by the IK / planning / collision functions (lazily, cached per process).

Public functions of :mod:`services.humanoid.g1`.

at the joint configuration supplied with the call. Units: metres, radians, wxyz quaternions.

    hand_joints: optional Dex3 finger angles (no named frame depends on them; accepted for

symbols.name: solve_arm_ik
symbols.doc:
Collision-aware IK for one arm (cuRobo ``InverseKinematics``).

Args:
    side: ``"left"`` or ``"right"``.
    target_position_m: target of the end-effector origin in ``frame`` (metres).
    target_quaternion_wxyz: target orientation of the end-effector frame in ``frame``;
        ``None`` solves for position only.
    frame: ``"pelvis"`` or ``"torso"`` (``torso_link`` at ``current_joints``).
    current_joints: measured joints ``{name: rad}`` or a CANONICAL29 vector. Every joint not
        being solved for (other arm, legs, waist unless ``use_waist``) is held here; the arm's
        own values seed the solver. Missing joints are taken as 0 (see ``defaulted_joints``).
    use_waist: also solve the three waist joints, kept within yaw +-0.6, roll +-0.25 and
        pitch +-0.35 rad (``solvers.WAIST_LIMITS_RAD``).
    seeds: parallel optimisation seeds (cuRobo ``num_seeds``); each value builds a solver.
    end_effector: ``"palm"`` (``*_hand_palm_link``, default), ``"wrist"``
        (``*_wrist_yaw_link``) or ``"hand_center"`` (point between the open fingers and thumb).
    obstacles: cuboids in ``frame``: ``[{"cuboid": {"dims": [x, y, z],
        "pose_wxyz": [x, y, z, qw, qx, qy, qz]}}]`` (box centre pose, full edge lengths).
    hand_joints: optional Dex3 finger angles for the collision model (default open hand).

Returns:
    dict with ``success`` (cuRobo: converged within 5 mm / 0.05 rad, within joint limits,
    no self or obstacle collision), ``joints`` (solved joints), ``joints_canonical29``
    (current joints with the solution substituted, CANONICAL29 order), ``position_error_m``,
    ``rotation_error_rad`` (None for position-only; both recomputed with the NumPy FK of the
    returned joints), ``achieved_pose`` (in ``frame``), ``limit_violations``,
    ``solve_time_s`` (wall time of the cuRobo solve), ``call_time_s``,
    ``solver_build_time_s`` (non-zero on the call that built this solver variant),
    ``held_links_excluded_from_collision`` and ``moving_links_touching_obstacles_at_start``.

symbols.name: resample_trajectory
symbols.doc: Linearly resample a joint trajectory onto a uniform grid ``0, dt, 2dt, ..., T``.

symbols.name: plan_arm_motion
symbols.doc:
Collision-free, time-parameterised arm trajectory (cuRobo ``MotionPlanner``).

Same targets/obstacles/frames/end effectors as :func:`solve_arm_ik`. The trajectory starts
at the arm joints in ``current_joints`` (all other joints held there), ends at the target
(5 mm / 0.05 rad), and respects joint limits, self-collision and the cuboid obstacles
(1 cm margin) with acceleration <= 6 rad/s^2 and jerk <= 100 rad/s^3 per joint before
``time_scale`` (typical reaches peak at 1-1.5 rad/s).

Args:
    control_dt_s: output sample period (default 0.02 s = the 50 Hz control tick).
    time_scale: >= 1 retimes the same path uniformly slower (2.0 = twice as long, half speed).
    max_attempts: cuRobo planning attempts.

Returns:
    dict with ``success``, ``status``, ``joint_names`` (solved joints), ``times_s``,
    ``positions`` (one row per sample, rad), ``velocities`` (rad/s), ``dt_s``,
    ``duration_s``, ``final_joints``, ``trajectory_canonical29`` (one 29-vector per sample in
    CANONICAL29 order; held joints from ``current_joints``), ``position_error_m``,
    ``rotation_error_rad``, ``achieved_pose``, ``max_abs_velocity_rad_s``,
    ``limit_violations`` and timing fields.

Uses the same sphere model as the solvers (obstacles get the 1 cm margin; link pairs at most
two joints apart are not checked against each other). Returns ``{"self_collision": bool,
"obstacle_collision": bool, "self_penetration_m": deepest sphere-pair overlap,
"obstacle_penetration_sum_m": summed sphere penetration into obstacles,

summary:
Persistent caches for cuRobo's runtime-compiled CUDA kernels.

cuRobo v0.8.0 compiles its CUDA kernels at runtime with NVRTC (``cuda.core`` backend, the
supported path; the deprecated pybind extension build is incomplete in this release) and
keeps them only in process memory. Warp kernels are JIT-compiled into a disk cache.
Neither needs nvcc or network access, but recompiling in every new process costs seconds.

``install()`` (called before cuRobo is imported) adds two read-through caches:

* cuRobo NVRTC kernels: cubins keyed exactly as cuRobo keys them (SHA-256 of the kernel
  source, kernel name, flags and GPU arch). Lookup order: the read-only cache prebuilt at
  install time inside this package (``prebuilt/curobo``), then a per-user cache
  (``$HUMANOID_G1_CACHE`` or ``$XDG_CACHE_HOME/humanoid-g1`` or ``~/.cache/humanoid-g1``). Misses
  are compiled with NVRTC as usual and written to the per-user cache.
* Warp: the per-user warp kernel directory is seeded from ``prebuilt/warp-<version>`` once.
* PyTorch's jiterator kernels (cuRobo's samplers use ``torch.erfinv``): ``PYTORCH_KERNEL_CACHE_PATH``
  points to a per-user directory seeded from ``prebuilt/torch-kernels`` (unless already set).

If anything about these caches fails, cuRobo's own in-memory compilation is used unchanged.

symbols.doc:
Writable per-user cache: $HUMANOID_G1_CACHE, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/humanoid-g1, ~/.cache/humanoid-g1,

summary:
cuRobo-backed arm IK, motion planning and collision queries for the G1 + Dex3.

CUDA, torch and cuRobo are imported on the first call only; built solvers are cached for
the life of the process (one per kind / side / waist option / end effector / position-only),
so repeated calls only pay the solve time.

Locked joints. Every joint that is not being solved for (the other arm, the legs, the
waist unless ``use_waist=True`` and the Dex3 fingers) is a *locked* joint in the cuRobo
model, held at the caller's measured ``current_joints``. cuRobo turns a locked joint into a
fixed transform ``parent_T_child = origin * Rot(axis, q)``; this module rewrites those
transforms in place before every call (the cuRobo-supported way to change locked-joint
state without rebuilding, see ``Kinematics.update_kinematics_config``), so the same CUDA
graphs serve any posture. ``self_check()`` verifies this against a freshly built model.

G1 + Dex3 semantic40 action and observation contract (dependency-light).

The action is HumanoidArena's canonical 40-value whole-body frame at 50 Hz, tracked by the
frozen SONIC whole-body controller (encoder mode 0). Layout and semantics follow the pinned
upstream converter (``isaaclab_twist2_g1/action_provider``): the controller receives only the
29 joint angles [9:38], their tick-to-tick change, and the root rotation [3:9] relative to the
measured pelvis. Root XY [0:2] and height [2] are part of the layout but do not move the robot:
it translates only by stepping, through the leg joint references.

Observations carry only HumanoidArena's policy inputs: the front camera, the 29 joint states,
the root orientation and the Dex3 finger state. No world position and no object state.

The pinned inference profile spawns the door as AssetBaseCfg. IsaacLab's scene

summary:
Upstream's fall rule (HumanoidArena ``script/eval_scripts/sonic/sim_eval_vla.py``).

A control step is a fall candidate when the root's up axis tilts more than 75 degrees, or more
than 60 degrees while a critical body (pelvis, torso, waist, hip, thigh, knee, calf, shin or
head, but not ankle or foot) carries at least 50 N of contact force. A fall is declared after
5 consecutive candidate steps. Contact forces come from ``robot.data.body_net_contact_force_w``
exactly as upstream reads them; when that field is absent the contact branch is inactive, as
it is upstream. Success is checked before falls, also as upstream does.

symbols.name: FallDetector
symbols.doc: Streak-confirmed fall state across the control steps of one episode.

summary:
Football goal collider: the goal net collides as its exact triangle mesh (always on for football_single).

Upstream's goal asset (football_goal/football_goal_physics.usd) collides through convexDecomposition.
Isaac Sim 6.1's PhysX cooks one of its hulls across the goal mouth: an invisible flat step 5.4 cm above
the turf and 15 cm deep, while the drawn ground bar lies below the turf. The same decomposition puts a
low ceiling inside the goal and makes the posts wider than drawn and asymmetric. The HumanoidArena
paper (arXiv 2606.17833) describes a kinematic goal net and no step. Whether Isaac Sim 5.0, upstream's
version, cooks the same hull is unverified.

Here the goal mesh collides as the exact triangle mesh
(approximation "none", which PhysX supports on the kinematic body upstream declares). Upstream files
stay unchanged: the instanced goal geometry becomes ordinary prims of the live stage, where the
approximation is authored, and PhysX reads it when the simulation is reset (parsed again). Pose, body
flags, contact offsets, materials, the ball, the rendering and the success predicate stay upstream's.

symbols.name: goal_entities
symbols.doc: (scene entity, prim path expression, asset) of every entity spawned from upstream's goal asset.

symbols.name: use_exact_goal_mesh
symbols.doc:
Author triangle-mesh collision on the goal meshes of the live stage and return what changed.

Call before the simulation is reset: PhysX reads the change only when it parses the stage again.

summary:
humanoid_free_space_move: cuRobo arm plans executed as semantic40 frames.

The plan starts at the measured arm joints and avoids self-collision only (the planner knows
no scene objects). Each 50 Hz trajectory sample becomes one semantic40 frame: the planned arm
(and, with use_waist, waist) joints; every other joint, both hands, the root rotation and root
height held at the last commanded frame (at the measured state before any command). The legs
therefore keep their references and the robot does not step.

symbols.name: held_frame
symbols.doc: The frame the plan holds: the last commanded one, or one built from the measured state.

summary:
Isaac Sim 6.1 physics sync for upstream's seeded prim-pose resets (outside the upstream sources).

Upstream ``common_env_objects._write_prim_world_pose`` writes each sampled pose into an
``xformOp:transform`` appended after the prim's authored translate/orient/scale ops, so USD
composes it with them. On the DoubleDesk basket and the navigation sign (authored in
centimetres, scale 0.01) the sampled translation therefore shrinks a hundredfold while the
sampled yaw applies in full; the PnP shelf and the OpenDoor container (scale 1) land at their
authored position plus the sample. This is upstream's realized official layout: the official
expert recordings show the same poses, every success predicate reads the same composed pose,
and it is independent of the Isaac Sim version. The backend keeps it exactly, following the
official benchmark.

What does differ in Isaac Sim 6.1 is physics: PhysX builds a static collider when it parses
the stage and does not follow later USD edits. When upstream's reset has written a static
collider, the backend therefore restarts physics and replays the identical seeded reset, so
the colliders sit where the prims are rendered. Simulated bodies keep their PhysX state; the
OpenDoor door follows its composed container through its own adapter (door_reset.py).

symbols.name: _authored_local
symbols.doc: The prim's authored translate/orient/scale transform, without the appended matrix.

symbols.name: authored_world_pose
symbols.doc: World position and wxyz rotation of a prim's authored TRS ops, ignoring an appended op.

symbols.name: world_pose
symbols.doc: Composed world position and scale-free wxyz rotation of a prim (operator diagnostics).

symbols.name: _static_collider
symbols.doc: No rigid body or articulation in the subtree: PhysX built a static actor at parse time.

symbols.name: upstream_prim_resets
symbols.doc:
Report the poses upstream's reset wrote into USD; nothing is rewritten.

Each entry names the record, its prim, whether it is a static collider, whether upstream
wrote an appended transform this episode, and the composed world pose that results.

symbols.name: measure_static_footprints
symbols.doc:
Locate each written static collider in PhysX with downward rays around its rendered pose.

Records the centre of the ray hits on the prim's own colliders (a hollow object's open
interior lets rays through, so this estimates its footprint centre) and fails if PhysX
has no collider of that prim near where it is rendered.

sha256("<gym id>|<group seed>|<repeat>"), big-endian, masked to a positive int32, and the
environment resets objects from that seed (``object_reset_seed_source: env_seed``). Upstream
ends an episode after ``MAX_STEPS`` 50 Hz control steps.

summary:
Model of the robot you control: Unitree G1 (29 body joints) with two Dex3 hands.

Everything here comes from ``robot.json`` next to this file, which was exported from the
simulated robot itself (its USD articulation) and checked against the simulator's measured
link poses. Pure Python 3.6+; NumPy and Pillow are used when present.

An observation is the JSON of an observe or motion reply (its first text block), saved to a
file; a saved frame-sequence manifest works too (its last frame is used). Quick start::

    S=.agents/skills/robot-interface/scripts
    python3 $S/g1_model.py pose --observation obs.json             # key points, level frame
    python3 $S/g1_model.py pose --observation obs.json --png /tmp/pose.png   # stick figure
    python3 $S/g1_model.py deproject 320 300 --observation obs.json --depth-png frame_depth.png
    python3 $S/g1_model.py project 0.45 -0.2 -0.1 --observation obs.json   # level frame -> pixel
    python3 $S/g1_model.py semantic40      # what every action dimension controls
    python3 $S/g1_model.py hand            # Dex3 joints, open/closed poses, fingertips

From Python::

    import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".agents/skills/robot-interface/scripts")
    import g1_model as g1
    pose = g1.pose_from_observation(g1.load_observation("obs.json"))   # or g1.MODEL.fk(joints29, ...)
    pose.point("right_hand_center", frame="level")            # metres, wxyz
    pose.deproject(u, v, depth_m, frame="level")               # depth = distance to image plane

Frames (all metres, quaternions [w, x, y, z]):

- ``pelvis``: the robot root body (the observation's root orientation is this body's
  orientation). x forward, y left, z up.
- ``level``: same origin as ``pelvis``, but gravity-aligned: z points straight up and x is the
  pelvis forward direction projected onto the horizontal plane. Needs the root orientation;
  without it ``level`` equals ``pelvis``. Heights in ``level`` are relative to the pelvis origin.
- any link name, ``camera`` (``d435_link``: x along the optical axis, y left, z up) and
  ``camera_optical`` (x right, y down, z forward: the image/depth frame).

There is no world frame: nothing here knows where the robot or any object is in the room.

summary:
The agent CLI on the host: its sandbox paths, robot-tool socket, environment and processes.

Codex and Claude Code run natively with their own logins and reach their model providers
directly. Each CLI's own sandbox confines the commands the agent runs: writes only in its
workspace, no internet, no host processes, and the repository, every session's private
files and the host's sockets unreadable. The session's frontend serves the robot tools on
a Unix socket; the CLI reaches it through mcp_bridge.py, the agent's Python through
RAX_MCP_SOCKET (auto_research_agent/api/runtime.py).

symbols.name: socket_path
symbols.doc:
The session's robot socket, alone in its own directory: the sandbox exposes that
directory and hides every other session's (Linux socket paths are limited to 107 bytes).

symbols.name: agent_python
symbols.doc:
The interpreter on the agent's PATH: this environment by its real path, since the
repository path that links to it is hidden from the sandbox.

symbols.name: host_secrets
symbols.doc:
The operator's credentials under their home: SECRETS and every other Codex home's login
(~/.codex-*/auth.json). Few, whole directories: Claude Code's sandbox command grows with every
path it hides, and fails beyond about a hundred of them.

symbols.name: reexposed_paths
symbols.doc:
Readable inside hidden directories: the Python environments in the runtime (the agent's
Python among them) and Codex's own install, which Codex runs inside its sandbox.

symbols.name: _exists
symbols.doc: Whether a path exists; one this user cannot even stat is as unreadable to the agent.

symbols.name: hidden_paths
symbols.doc:
What the agent's commands must not read: the repository, the assets, checkouts and
runtime it links to (except the Python environments), every session's directory (the
agent's own workspace is re-exposed writable), the other robot sockets, host sockets and
the operator's credentials.

carved: for a sandbox (Codex's) that cannot make a path readable again inside a hidden one,
a hidden directory holding a reexposed_paths() entry, or one of ``kept`` (the session's
reference data), is replaced by its other entries.

symbols.doc:
``path`` to hide, or, when it holds a ``kept`` path, its entries but that one, carved likewise.
An entry that links outside ``path`` is not part of it and is left out.

Start the agent CLI under supervise() (this file, run isolated from the workspace's

symbols.name: supervise
symbols.doc:
Run the agent CLI and, once it exits, end everything it left running. This process
adopts the CLI's orphaned descendants (a child subreaper), so a background command that
outlived the CLI is still found. Returns the CLI's exit status.

symbols.name: descendants
symbols.doc: Every live process below `pid` (the CLI's sandboxed commands included).

symbols.name: signal_tree
symbols.doc: Signal a process and its descendants, walking again until no new one appears.

symbols.name: start_time
symbols.doc: The kernel's start time of `pid`, which tells it apart from a later process reusing the id.

symbols.doc: Write the agent's pid file for the frontend (frozen()).

symbols.doc: True once the kernel has stopped `pid` (or it is gone).

symbols.name: frozen
symbols.doc:
Stop the agent CLI and everything it runs for the block: a background writer must not

summary:
The dedicated Claude account for experiments: its setup-token and identity.

Experiments never use the operator's personal Claude login (~/.claude). A separate
account signs in once in its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and issues a long-lived
``claude setup-token`` token. Sessions sign Claude Code in with only that token
(login.Credential):

    ~/.config/rax/                  (0700; RAX_CLAUDE_EXPERIMENT_DIR overrides)
      claude-experiment-home/            dedicated CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, for sign-in only
      claude-experiment.token            the token (0600), read at each launch
      claude-experiment.json             identity (0600): email, organization, created_at

Every claude-login launch and resume reads that one token file, so a rotated token applies
from a session's next launch.

Set up or rotate with ``bash scripts/setup_claude_experiment_login.sh``.

symbols.doc: Signed-in account of a Claude config dir (None: the operator's default login).

symbols.name: install
symbols.doc: Store the experiment token (0600) and its non-secret identity.

symbols.doc: Presence and identity without network access (dashboard and preflight).

symbols.doc: Best effort: the account behind the token (Claude Code's OAuth profile endpoint).

symbols.doc:
status() plus a free count_tokens call proving the token is accepted.

When the profile endpoint names the token's account, it must be the recorded
experiment account and must not be the operator's personal login.

symbols.doc:
The experiment account's subscription usage, from the rate-limit headers of a one-token

Native sessions have no relay to see a usage-limit refusal, so a launcher asks after a run ends.

When an exhausted usage window reopens: the reset of a 429 refusal whose unified status is
`rejected` (ten minutes on when it names none). None for any other answer, an ordinary 429, a
rejected token or an unreachable API included: the next run reports those itself.

Episode reviews: an operator-side analyst's review of each finished exploration episode.

The lifecycle is shared by every benchmark whose simulator writes ground truth
(``services.benchmarks``: ``episode_reviews``):

- ``runner``: settings (off, on, detailed) in ``<session>/operator-analysis/settings.json``,
  background workers that wait for a closed episode's simulator files, the Gemini call through
  the OpenRouter router, the cost ledger, the 0600 operator record and the agent's

- ``common``: helpers every benchmark's analysis uses (condensed tool trace, final RGB frames,
  the Gemini call, the budget).
- ``workspace``: the TASK.md "Episode reviews" section and the AGENTS.md reminder.

A benchmark supplies its ground truth and wording through its adapter hook
``review_analysis()``, a module with:

- ``ground_truth_report(sim_dir)``: the report of one finished episode (a dict whose
  ``episode_id`` and ``episode_mode`` name it), or None when the simulator wrote nothing;
- ``condensed_trace(mcp_trace)``: one line per tool call;
- ``explain(router, report, trace, images, *, task_instruction, detailed, score)``:
  the analyst's explanation and its cost, ``(text, cost_usd)``;
- ``agent_review(report, explanation, *, episode_number, detailed, score, run)``: the
  agent-safe Markdown of ``review.md``;
- ``task_instruction(task)``: the task's instruction for the analyst.

Reviews are part of closing an episode: the session's episode management (the supervisor
for single-environment episodes and rehearsals, the exploration pool for parallel ones)
reports each closed episode to the session's ``EpisodeReviews``, owned by its MCP service
(``services.controller.frontend``), so no dashboard is involved. While the operator has
reviews on, every closed exploration or rehearsal episode gets one review from the
session's benchmark's analysis (its adapter's ``review_analysis()``, see

- the operator record: ``<session>/operator-analysis/<episode_id>.json`` (0600), never

- the agent's copy: ``review.md`` in that episode's own published run directory (the
  ``artifacts.directory`` its ``finish`` or ``rehearse`` reply named), which the agent reads
  read-only under ``runtime/autonomous_controller/runs/`` in its workspace. TASK.md says where.

Formal episodes are never reviewed. Gemini costs go to ``operator-analysis/usage.jsonl``
and never to the agent's own budget.

summary:
G1 + Dex3 kinematics (numpy) and cuRobo, arm IK and motion planning, used by humanoid_free_space_move.

Body-frame only. Every pose is expressed in the ``pelvis`` frame (the articulation root,
default) or in the ``torso_link`` frame (``frame="torso"``), evaluated at the joint
configuration you pass. Metres, radians, quaternions ``[w, x, y, z]``. Joint names are the
simulator's canonical names (:data:`CANONICAL29`).

Quick reference::

    from services.humanoid import g1
    fk = g1.forward_kinematics(joints)                 # named frame poses, CPU only
    table = {"cuboid": {"dims": [0.5, 1.2, 0.04], "pose_wxyz": [0.55, 0, -0.02, 1, 0, 0, 0]}}
    ik = g1.solve_arm_ik("right", [0.35, -0.2, 0.08], [0.7071068, -0.7071068, 0, 0],
                         current_joints=joints, end_effector="hand_center", obstacles=[table])
    plan = g1.plan_arm_motion("right", [0.35, -0.2, 0.08], [0.7071068, -0.7071068, 0, 0],
                              current_joints=joints, end_effector="hand_center", obstacles=[table])

CUDA is only initialised by the IK / planning / collision functions (lazily, cached per process).

Public functions of :mod:`services.humanoid.g1`.

Frames: ``"pelvis"`` (articulation root, default) or ``"torso"`` (``torso_link``), both taken
at the joint configuration supplied with the call. Units: metres, radians, wxyz quaternions.

symbols.name: _base_T_frame
symbols.doc: pelvis_T_frame for frame in FRAMES at ``joints``.

symbols.name: forward_kinematics
symbols.doc:
Poses of named frames for one joint configuration.

Args:
    joints: ``{joint_name: rad}`` (missing joints are taken as 0 and listed in
        ``defaulted_joints``) or a 29-vector in :data:`CANONICAL29` order.
    frames: names from :data:`NAMED_FRAMES` (default: all of them).
    hand_joints: optional Dex3 finger angles (no named frame depends on them; accepted for
        symmetry with the collision functions).
    backend: ``"numpy"`` (CPU, no CUDA) or ``"curobo"`` (cuRobo GPU kinematics, same URDF).

Returns:
    ``{"pelvis": {frame: {"position_m", "quaternion_wxyz"}}, "torso": {...},
    "defaulted_joints": [...], "backend": ...}``

symbols.name: transform_pose
symbols.doc:
Re-express a point/pose given in one named frame in another, at ``joints``.

Example: a point measured from the depth image in the ROS optical frame of the front
camera -> pelvis frame: ``transform_pose(p_cam, from_frame="camera_optical")``.

symbols.name: solve_arm_ik
symbols.doc:
Collision-aware IK for one arm (cuRobo ``InverseKinematics``).

Args:
    side: ``"left"`` or ``"right"``.
    target_position_m: target of the end-effector origin in ``frame`` (metres).
    target_quaternion_wxyz: target orientation of the end-effector frame in ``frame``;
        ``None`` solves for position only.
    frame: ``"pelvis"`` or ``"torso"`` (``torso_link`` at ``current_joints``).
    current_joints: measured joints ``{name: rad}`` or a CANONICAL29 vector. Every joint not
        being solved for (other arm, legs, waist unless ``use_waist``) is held here; the arm's
        own values seed the solver. Missing joints are taken as 0 (see ``defaulted_joints``).
    use_waist: also solve the three waist joints, kept within yaw +-0.6, roll +-0.25 and
        pitch +-0.35 rad (``solvers.WAIST_LIMITS_RAD``).
    seeds: parallel optimisation seeds (cuRobo ``num_seeds``); each value builds a solver.
    end_effector: ``"palm"`` (``*_hand_palm_link``, default), ``"wrist"``
        (``*_wrist_yaw_link``) or ``"hand_center"`` (point between the open fingers and thumb).
    obstacles: cuboids in ``frame``: ``[{"cuboid": {"dims": [x, y, z],
        "pose_wxyz": [x, y, z, qw, qx, qy, qz]}}]`` (box centre pose, full edge lengths).
    hand_joints: optional Dex3 finger angles for the collision model (default open hand).

Returns:
    dict with ``success`` (cuRobo: converged within 5 mm / 0.05 rad, within joint limits,
    no self or obstacle collision), ``joints`` (solved joints), ``joints_canonical29``
    (current joints with the solution substituted, CANONICAL29 order), ``position_error_m``,
    ``rotation_error_rad`` (None for position-only; both recomputed with the NumPy FK of the
    returned joints), ``achieved_pose`` (in ``frame``), ``limit_violations``,
    ``solve_time_s`` (wall time of the cuRobo solve), ``call_time_s``,
    ``solver_build_time_s`` (non-zero on the call that built this solver variant),
    ``held_links_excluded_from_collision`` and ``moving_links_touching_obstacles_at_start``.

symbols.name: resample_trajectory
symbols.doc: Linearly resample a joint trajectory onto a uniform grid ``0, dt, 2dt, ..., T``.

symbols.name: plan_arm_motion
symbols.doc:
Collision-free, time-parameterised arm trajectory (cuRobo ``MotionPlanner``).

Same targets/obstacles/frames/end effectors as :func:`solve_arm_ik`. The trajectory starts
at the arm joints in ``current_joints`` (all other joints held there), ends at the target
(5 mm / 0.05 rad), and respects joint limits, self-collision and the cuboid obstacles
(1 cm margin) with acceleration <= 6 rad/s^2 and jerk <= 100 rad/s^3 per joint before
``time_scale`` (typical reaches peak at 1-1.5 rad/s).

Args:
    control_dt_s: output sample period (default 0.02 s = the 50 Hz control tick).
    time_scale: >= 1 retimes the same path uniformly slower (2.0 = twice as long, half speed).
    max_attempts: cuRobo planning attempts.

Returns:
    dict with ``success``, ``status``, ``joint_names`` (solved joints), ``times_s``,
    ``positions`` (one row per sample, rad), ``velocities`` (rad/s), ``dt_s``,
    ``duration_s``, ``final_joints``, ``trajectory_canonical29`` (one 29-vector per sample in
    CANONICAL29 order; held joints from ``current_joints``), ``position_error_m``,
    ``rotation_error_rad``, ``achieved_pose``, ``max_abs_velocity_rad_s``,
    ``limit_violations`` and timing fields.

symbols.name: check_collision
symbols.doc:
Self- and obstacle-collision check of one full-body configuration (cuRobo spheres).

Uses the same sphere model as the solvers (obstacles get the 1 cm margin; link pairs at most
two joints apart are not checked against each other). Returns ``{"self_collision": bool,
"obstacle_collision": bool, "self_penetration_m": deepest sphere-pair overlap,
"obstacle_penetration_sum_m": summed sphere penetration into obstacles,
"links_touching_obstacles": {link: depth_m}}``.

Build (and run once) the requested solvers so later calls in this process only pay solve

summary:
Persistent caches for cuRobo's runtime-compiled CUDA kernels.

cuRobo v0.8.0 compiles its CUDA kernels at runtime with NVRTC (``cuda.core`` backend, the
supported path; the deprecated pybind extension build is incomplete in this release) and
keeps them only in process memory. Warp kernels are JIT-compiled into a disk cache.
Neither needs nvcc or network access, but recompiling in every new process costs seconds.

``install()`` (called before cuRobo is imported) adds two read-through caches:

* cuRobo NVRTC kernels: cubins keyed exactly as cuRobo keys them (SHA-256 of the kernel
  source, kernel name, flags and GPU arch). Lookup order: the read-only cache prebuilt at
  install time inside this package (``prebuilt/curobo``), then a per-user cache
  (``$HUMANOID_G1_CACHE`` or ``$XDG_CACHE_HOME/humanoid-g1`` or ``~/.cache/humanoid-g1``). Misses
  are compiled with NVRTC as usual and written to the per-user cache.
* Warp: the per-user warp kernel directory is seeded from ``prebuilt/warp-<version>`` once.
* PyTorch's jiterator kernels (cuRobo's samplers use ``torch.erfinv``): ``PYTORCH_KERNEL_CACHE_PATH``
  points to a per-user directory seeded from ``prebuilt/torch-kernels`` (unless already set).

If anything about these caches fails, cuRobo's own in-memory compilation is used unchanged.

symbols.name: user_cache_dir
symbols.doc:
Writable per-user cache: $HUMANOID_G1_CACHE, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/humanoid-g1, ~/.cache/humanoid-g1,
else <tmp>/humanoid-g1-<uid>.

symbols.name: _seed
symbols.doc: Copy a prebuilt cache directory into a writable one, once.

summary:
cuRobo-backed arm IK, motion planning and collision queries for the G1 + Dex3.

CUDA, torch and cuRobo are imported on the first call only; built solvers are cached for
the life of the process (one per kind / side / waist option / end effector / position-only),
so repeated calls only pay the solve time.

Locked joints. Every joint that is not being solved for (the other arm, the legs, the
waist unless ``use_waist=True`` and the Dex3 fingers) is a *locked* joint in the cuRobo
model, held at the caller's measured ``current_joints``. cuRobo turns a locked joint into a
fixed transform ``parent_T_child = origin * Rot(axis, q)``; this module rewrites those
transforms in place before every call (the cuRobo-supported way to change locked-joint
state without rebuilding, see ``Kinematics.update_kinematics_config``), so the same CUDA
graphs serve any posture. ``self_check()`` verifies this against a freshly built model.

symbols.name: runtime
symbols.doc: Import torch/cuRobo once, after installing the persistent kernel caches.

symbols.name: _chain_joints

symbols.name: self_collision_ignore
symbols.doc:
Shipped ignore matrix + close kinematic neighbours + pairs that cannot move relatively.

With ``active_joints`` fixed for the solve, two links whose chains contain the same active
joints keep a constant relative pose (it only depends on locked joints), so they are ignored:
a self-contact among held joints (e.g. legs vs pelvis at the measured posture) must not make
every arm solution infeasible.

summary:
G1 + Dex3 semantic40 action and observation contract (dependency-light).

The action is HumanoidArena's canonical 40-value whole-body frame at 50 Hz, tracked by the
frozen SONIC whole-body controller (encoder mode 0). Layout and semantics follow the pinned
upstream converter (``isaaclab_twist2_g1/action_provider``): the controller receives only the
29 joint angles [9:38], their tick-to-tick change, and the root rotation [3:9] relative to the
measured pelvis. Root XY [0:2] and height [2] are part of the layout but do not move the robot:
it translates only by stepping, through the leg joint references.

Observations carry only HumanoidArena's policy inputs: the front camera, the 29 joint states,
the root orientation and the Dex3 finger state. No world position and no object state.

Reset-only support for Arena's unmanaged inference-profile door articulation.

The pinned inference profile spawns the door as AssetBaseCfg. IsaacLab's scene
reset therefore resets the robot, but does not restore the physical door joints.
This adapter preserves the initial physical state and applies it only at episode

summary:
Upstream's fall rule (HumanoidArena ``script/eval_scripts/sonic/sim_eval_vla.py``).

A control step is a fall candidate when the root's up axis tilts more than 75 degrees, or more
than 60 degrees while a critical body (pelvis, torso, waist, hip, thigh, knee, calf, shin or
head, but not ankle or foot) carries at least 50 N of contact force. A fall is declared after
5 consecutive candidate steps. Contact forces come from ``robot.data.body_net_contact_force_w``
exactly as upstream reads them; when that field is absent the contact branch is inactive, as
it is upstream. Success is checked before falls, also as upstream does.

symbols.name: FallDetector
symbols.doc: Streak-confirmed fall state across the control steps of one episode.

summary:
Football goal collider: the goal net collides as its exact triangle mesh (always on for football_single).

Upstream's goal asset (football_goal/football_goal_physics.usd) collides through convexDecomposition.
Isaac Sim 6.1's PhysX cooks one of its hulls across the goal mouth: an invisible flat step 5.4 cm above
the turf and 15 cm deep, while the drawn ground bar lies below the turf. The same decomposition puts a
low ceiling inside the goal and makes the posts wider than drawn and asymmetric. The HumanoidArena
paper (arXiv 2606.17833) describes a kinematic goal net and no step. Whether Isaac Sim 5.0, upstream's
version, cooks the same hull is unverified.

Here the goal mesh collides as the exact triangle mesh
(approximation "none", which PhysX supports on the kinematic body upstream declares). Upstream files
stay unchanged: the instanced goal geometry becomes ordinary prims of the live stage, where the
approximation is authored, and PhysX reads it when the simulation is reset (parsed again). Pose, body
flags, contact offsets, materials, the ball, the rendering and the success predicate stay upstream's.

symbols.name: goal_entities
symbols.doc: (scene entity, prim path expression, asset) of every entity spawned from upstream's goal asset.

symbols.name: use_exact_goal_mesh
symbols.doc:
Author triangle-mesh collision on the goal meshes of the live stage and return what changed.

Call before the simulation is reset: PhysX reads the change only when it parses the stage again.

summary:
humanoid_free_space_move: cuRobo arm plans executed as semantic40 frames.

The plan starts at the measured arm joints and avoids self-collision only (the planner knows
no scene objects). Each 50 Hz trajectory sample becomes one semantic40 frame: the planned arm
(and, with use_waist, waist) joints; every other joint, both hands, the root rotation and root
height held at the last commanded frame (at the measured state before any command). The legs
therefore keep their references and the robot does not step.

symbols.name: held_frame

summary:
Isaac Sim 6.1 physics sync for upstream's seeded prim-pose resets (outside the upstream sources).

Upstream ``common_env_objects._write_prim_world_pose`` writes each sampled pose into an
``xformOp:transform`` appended after the prim's authored translate/orient/scale ops, so USD
composes it with them. On the DoubleDesk basket and the navigation sign (authored in
centimetres, scale 0.01) the sampled translation therefore shrinks a hundredfold while the
sampled yaw applies in full; the PnP shelf and the OpenDoor container (scale 1) land at their
authored position plus the sample. This is upstream's realized official layout: the official
expert recordings show the same poses, every success predicate reads the same composed pose,
and it is independent of the Isaac Sim version. The backend keeps it exactly, following the
official benchmark.

What does differ in Isaac Sim 6.1 is physics: PhysX builds a static collider when it parses
the stage and does not follow later USD edits. When upstream's reset has written a static
collider, the backend therefore restarts physics and replays the identical seeded reset, so
the colliders sit where the prims are rendered. Simulated bodies keep their PhysX state; the
OpenDoor door follows its composed container through its own adapter (door_reset.py).

Experiments never use the operator's personal Claude login (~/.claude). A separate
account signs in once in its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and issues a long-lived
``claude setup-token`` token. The relay (messages_relay.Credential) reads only
that token file:

    ~/.config/rax/                  (0700; RAX_CLAUDE_EXPERIMENT_DIR overrides)

      claude-experiment.token            the token (0600), re-read by the relay per request
      claude-experiment.json             identity (0600): email, organization, created_at

Every claude-login session's relay reads that one token file, so a rotated token applies to
running sessions at once.

Set up or rotate with ``bash scripts/setup_claude_experiment_login.sh``.

finished and it was never scored, so a fresh copy of the same frozen checkpoint plays that
layout from the start. The stopped attempt moves from the results to the batch's
interruptions record and its worker folder moves aside, so every reader of the results and
worker folders sees one episode per layout.

One LIBERO-PRO episode inside the simulator process (runs in runtime/envs/libero_pro, Python 3.8).

The official ``OffScreenRenderEnv`` (libero.libero.envs) owns the scene, robot, controller, physics,
rendering and the success check, built from the official BDDL of the layout's collection. Episodes
start as the public LIBERO evaluation runner starts them: ``env.seed``, ``reset``, the official init
state (formal), then 10 no-op steps with the gripper open for objects to settle. The agent's rows go
to ``env.step``; the episode ends when ``step`` reports done (LIBERO: the BDDL goal holds) or at the
suite's step limit. Exploration layouts are fresh seeded resets of the original BDDL.

The session adds the harness contract: identity-checked RPC ops, agent observations (the two
cameras upright at 256x256, optional depth from robosuite's get_real_depth_map and calibration,
the runners' 8-D state, the BDDL instruction) and the trusted operator files. Object poses, the
layout and the collection stay in operator-only files.

they are formal layout collections of the same task, so one exploration session is scored on the

- Collection 1 (official LIBERO): the original BDDL and its 50 official init states.
- Collections 2-5 (LIBERO-PRO): the perturbed BDDL and its 50 init states from the official

  size variants), 4 language (paraphrased instruction), 5 task (a new goal in the same scene).

summary: Agent workspace generation: recipes (per role) + setup facts -> files.

One pipeline for every agent workspace: sources + recipe + setup -> files.

build() copies the recipe's template and skill layers, applies its role (documents,
variants, left-out skills and files), renders every markdown source against the
setup, and writes the tool contract. Callers add the session's extras (TASK.md,
demonstrations, CLI entry files) around it.

symbols.name: apply_role

symbols.name: manifest

summary:
A recipe says which sources make one kind of workspace (a role).

Recipes are values: a role is another recipe derived with dataclasses.replace, so
the exploration and formal-copy workspaces share everything they do not override.

symbols.name: Vocab
symbols.doc: Named words a shared source uses instead of spelling out paths and tool names.

symbols.doc: Leave a skill out when `when(setup)` holds.

summary: The facts a workspace is generated from; roles live in recipes, not here.

symbols.doc:
Which skill layers a workspace takes: the robot it controls, how it perceives and whether it
