symbols.doc: Template variables: facts only, named for readability in the sources.

summary:
Jinja rendering of trusted workspace sources.

Sources are markdown with Jinja statements on their own lines, e.g.

    {% if camera_geometry %}
    ...text for depth-capable profiles...
    {% else %}
    ...RGB-only text...
    {% endif %}

trim_blocks/lstrip_blocks drop the statement lines entirely, so rendered text keeps
the source's line layout. Unknown names fail the build (StrictUndefined).

Reusable passages are registered blocks (agent_blocks/blocks.toml) inserted with
{{ block("<id>") }} on a line of its own; the setup's facts, the recipe's `vocab`
and any keyword parameters are available inside a block. Every block a file uses
is recorded, so a build can report which blocks produced each file.

symbols.name: registry
symbols.doc: Block id -> entry; ids are unique and every path exists.

symbols.name: tidy
symbols.doc: Collapse blank-line runs left by empty conditionals; fenced examples stay verbatim.

symbols.name: render
symbols.doc: Render one source. `used`, when given, collects the block ids it inserted.

summary:
Checks a built workspace must pass, whatever its role.

Each rule reads the rendered files (not the sources) and returns human-readable
problems. Rules are deliberately narrow: they catch contradictions that reviews
found in practice (broken links, text for another setup, tool names the session
does not have) rather than judging prose.

symbols.name: prose
symbols.doc:
Text outside fenced examples; each example leaves its line breaks, so reported line
numbers stay those of the file.

symbols.name: markdown
symbols.doc:
Markdown files of the workspace itself: links inside it are not followed, but the
workspace path may lead through links (an agent-storage mount, a linked TMPDIR).

Every rule for one built workspace, given the setup facts it was built from.

summary:
Stdlib MCP client for robot and Gemini calls from Python.

`Context()` connects ordinary Python to the same MCP tools you call directly.
`main()` instead runs a controller's `main(ctx)` over standard input and output, with
the robot and Gemini tools only; there, Python prints are logged and native or
subprocess output goes to stderr.

symbols.name: PrintLog
symbols.doc: Keep Python prints separate from both MCP results and stderr.

symbols.name: __init__
symbols.doc: Connect ordinary Python to the MCP tools, or use the given reader and writer.

symbols.name: env
symbols.doc: A context whose robot and episode calls go to exploration environment `env_id`.

summary:
The agent CLI on the host: its sandbox paths, robot-tool socket, environment and processes.

Codex and Claude Code run natively with their own logins and reach their model providers
directly. Each CLI's own sandbox confines the commands the agent runs: writes only in its
workspace, no internet, no host processes, and the repository, every session's private
files and the host's sockets unreadable. The session's frontend serves the robot tools on
a Unix socket; the CLI reaches it through mcp_bridge.py, the agent's Python through
RAX_MCP_SOCKET (auto_research_agent/api/runtime.py).

symbols.name: socket_path
symbols.doc:
The session's robot socket, alone in its own directory: the sandbox exposes that
directory and hides every other session's (Linux socket paths are limited to 107 bytes).

symbols.name: agent_python
symbols.doc:
The interpreter on the agent's PATH: this environment by its real path, since the
repository path that links to it is hidden from the sandbox.

symbols.name: host_secrets
symbols.doc:
The operator's credentials under their home: SECRETS and every other Codex home's login
(~/.codex-*/auth.json). Few, whole directories: Claude Code's sandbox command grows with every
path it hides, and fails beyond about a hundred of them.

symbols.name: reexposed_paths
symbols.doc:
Readable inside hidden directories: the Python environments in the runtime (the agent's
Python among them) and Codex's own install, which Codex runs inside its sandbox.

symbols.name: _exists
symbols.doc: Whether a path exists; one this user cannot even stat is as unreadable to the agent.

symbols.name: hidden_paths
symbols.doc:
What the agent's commands must not read: the repository, the assets, checkouts and
runtime it links to (except the Python environments), every session's directory (the
agent's own workspace is re-exposed writable), the other robot sockets, host sockets and
the operator's credentials.

carved: for a sandbox (Codex's) that cannot make a path readable again inside a hidden one,
a hidden directory holding a reexposed_paths() entry, or one of ``kept`` (the session's
reference data), is replaced by its other entries.

symbols.name: carve
symbols.doc:
``path`` to hide, or, when it holds a ``kept`` path, its entries but that one, carved likewise.
An entry that links outside ``path`` is not part of it and is left out.

symbols.name: repositories
symbols.doc: This checkout and, for a git worktree, the repository it belongs to.

symbols.name: thread_variables
symbols.doc: Size math-library thread pools to the agent's share of the host, not every core.

symbols.name: environment
symbols.doc: The agent CLI's environment: nothing inherited but terminal and locale basics.

symbols.name: deprioritize
symbols.doc: preexec_fn for agent processes; inherited by everything the agent starts.

symbols.name: start
symbols.doc:
Start the agent CLI under supervise() (this file, run isolated from the workspace's
Python path). A non-interactive agent gets its own session.

symbols.name: supervise
symbols.doc:
Run the agent CLI and, once it exits, end everything it left running. This process
adopts the CLI's orphaned descendants (a child subreaper), so a background command that
outlived the CLI is still found. Returns the CLI's exit status.

symbols.name: descendants
symbols.doc: Every live process below `pid` (the CLI's sandboxed commands included).

symbols.name: signal_tree
symbols.doc: Signal a process and its descendants, walking again until no new one appears.

symbols.name: start_time
symbols.doc: The kernel's start time of `pid`, which tells it apart from a later process reusing the id.

symbols.name: record
symbols.doc: Write the agent's pid file for the frontend (frozen()).

symbols.name: recorded
symbols.doc: The live agent process named by a pid file, or None.

symbols.name: stopped
symbols.doc: True once the kernel has stopped `pid` (or it is gone).

symbols.name: frozen
symbols.doc:
Stop the agent CLI and everything it runs for the block: a background writer must not
change a submission while it is copied or executed. SIGSTOP reaches the parent first,
so nothing forks past the walk.

symbols.name: stop
symbols.doc: End the agent CLI started by start(); its supervisor ends what the CLI left running.

symbols.doc: Write the session's Claude Code home for this launch: settings, robot tools, trust.

symbols.doc:
Claude Code's process environment: its session home, its login, the robot socket and the

symbols.doc:
claude-login: when the experiment account's usage window resets, if a one-token probe of its
rate-limit headers finds it exhausted; None otherwise.

symbols.name: until_usage_resets
symbols.doc:
Run the agent. If the experiment account ran out of usage, wait for the reset (the frontend
and live episodes stay up), then continue the agent's own conversation.

symbols.doc:
The frontend, then native Claude Code in the workspace.

The frontend (the sole owner of the session's episodes) stays up for every agent run of this
launch: `agent_runs(run)` may call `run(prompt)` again after a run ends (a finished turn, an

summary:
The dedicated Claude account for experiments: its setup-token and identity.

Experiments never use the operator's personal Claude login (~/.claude). A separate
account signs in once in its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and issues a long-lived
``claude setup-token`` token. Sessions sign Claude Code in with only that token
(login.Credential):

    ~/.config/rax/                  (0700; RAX_CLAUDE_EXPERIMENT_DIR overrides)
      claude-experiment-home/            dedicated CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, for sign-in only
      claude-experiment.token            the token (0600), read at each launch
      claude-experiment.json             identity (0600): email, organization, created_at

Every claude-login launch and resume reads that one token file, so a rotated token applies
from a session's next launch.

Set up or rotate with ``bash scripts/setup_claude_experiment_login.sh``.

symbols.name: account
symbols.doc: Signed-in account of a Claude config dir (None: the operator's default login).

symbols.name: install
symbols.doc: Store the experiment token (0600) and its non-secret identity.

symbols.name: status
symbols.doc: Presence and identity without network access (dashboard and preflight).

symbols.name: token_account
symbols.doc: Best effort: the account behind the token (Claude Code's OAuth profile endpoint).

symbols.name: check
symbols.doc:
status() plus a free count_tokens call proving the token is accepted.

When the profile endpoint names the token's account, it must be the recorded
experiment account and must not be the operator's personal login.

symbols.name: usage
symbols.doc:
The experiment account's subscription usage, from the rate-limit headers of a one-token
Haiku call (setup tokens cannot read the usage endpoint; count_tokens carries no usage headers).
Native sessions have no relay to see a usage-limit refusal, so a launcher asks after a run ends.

symbols.name: usage_reset
symbols.doc:
When an exhausted usage window reopens: the reset of a 429 refusal whose unified status is
`rejected` (ten minutes on when it names none). None for any other answer, an ordinary 429, a
rejected token or an unreachable API included: the next run reports those itself.

summary:
Claude Code's login for a session: provider defaults and the credential Claude Code uses natively.

Providers:
- ``claude-login``: the dedicated experiment account's long-lived ``claude setup-token``
  token (harness/claude_cli/experiment_login.py), given to Claude Code as
  CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. The operator's personal Claude login (~/.claude) is refused.
- ``anthropic``: an Anthropic API key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY).
- ``openrouter``: OpenRouter's Anthropic-compatible endpoint with the OpenRouter key.
- ``custom``: a private Anthropic-compatible endpoint with its own bearer credential.

symbols.name: personal_login
symbols.doc: True for the operator's own Claude login, which experiments must never use.

symbols.name: Credential
symbols.doc: A provider credential, read from its file whenever it is used (a rotated token applies).

symbols.name: headers
symbols.doc: HTTP auth headers, for the harness's own account checks (experiment_login).

symbols.name: environment
symbols.doc: The variables that sign Claude Code in natively.

summary:

One bounded, never-fatal native agent invocation with a stub MCP endpoint that lists no
tools, so nothing in the environment can change. It writes the CLI's own compaction into
the same transcript, which later resumes continue from.

  the built-in command, the auto-compact threshold is lowered for one turn instead.

GPU placement is operator choice, not part of what a trial is. The session keeps it in three
copies (operator-input.json, configuration.json and the supervisor's state.json), which must

records a hash index. A refactor must reproduce the index byte for byte unless a
change is intended; `--out` writes the trees so two revisions can be diffed.

Usage:
  render_workspaces.py --index local_tests/goldens/workspaces.json   # write the index
  render_workspaces.py --check local_tests/goldens/workspaces.json   # compare
  render_workspaces.py --out DIR [--case NAME]                        # write trees

- ``condensed_trace(mcp_trace)``: one line per tool call;

- ``agent_review(report, explanation, *, episode_number, detailed, score, run)``: the

(upright, 256x256 JPEG), the actions and the 8-D state per step.

summary:
LIBERO-PRO simulator process: the official LIBERO environment for one episode.

Runs only in ``runtime/envs/libero_pro`` (Python 3.8, the official requirements) with the pinned
LIBERO-PRO checkout on PYTHONPATH and ``LIBERO_CONFIG_PATH`` at the runtime-owned config
(services/libero_pro/process.py).

One LIBERO-PRO episode inside the simulator process (runs in runtime/envs/libero_pro, Python 3.8).

The official ``OffScreenRenderEnv`` (libero.libero.envs) owns the scene, robot, controller, physics,
rendering and the success check, built from the official BDDL of the layout's collection. Episodes
start as the public LIBERO evaluation runner starts them: ``env.seed``, ``reset``, the official init
state (formal), then 10 no-op steps with the gripper open for objects to settle. The agent's rows go
to ``env.step``; the episode ends when ``step`` reports done (LIBERO: the BDDL goal holds) or at the
suite's step limit. Exploration layouts are fresh seeded resets of the original BDDL.

The session adds the harness contract: identity-checked RPC ops, agent observations (the two
cameras upright at 256x256, optional depth from robosuite's get_real_depth_map and calibration,
the runners' 8-D state, the BDDL instruction) and the trusted operator files. Object poses, the
layout and the collection stay in operator-only files.

summary:
LIBERO-PRO task catalog, layout collections and budgets (stdlib only; Python 3.8 compatible).

Each task of LIBERO's four ten-task suites (spatial, object, goal, libero_10) is one harness task,
``<suite>_<index>`` in the official suite order. LIBERO-PRO's perturbations are not separate tasks:
they are formal layout collections of the same task, so one exploration session is scored on the
official LIBERO layouts and, by post-hoc formal batches, under each perturbation.

- Collection 0 (exploration): the original BDDL, ``env.seed(1000 + i)`` then ``env.reset()``: fresh
  samples of the official placement distribution, never one of the stored evaluation states.
- Collection 1 (official LIBERO): the original BDDL and its 50 official init states.
- Collections 2-5 (LIBERO-PRO): the perturbed BDDL and its 50 init states from the official
  perturbation release: 2 swap (objects exchange initial regions), 3 object (object appearance and
  size variants), 4 language (paraphrased instruction), 5 task (a new goal in the same scene).

The environment perturbation was never released and has no collection.

summary:
Run Claude Code on the host as the robot agent, separated from the robot infrastructure.

The launcher (trusted, operator-run) prepares a session under the artifact root:

    <session>/
      configuration.json     operator configuration (services.controller.config)
      model-relay.json       provider, models and the credential *path* (never the token)
      agent-workspace/       the agent's cwd and its only writable directory
      claude-home/           CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and HOME of the agent: settings.json, mcp.json
      state.json, mcp.jsonl  robot-service ledger and audit log (unreadable to the agent)
      agent-lifecycle.json   launches, usage waits and exit status

and per launch starts two host services the agent cannot read or modify:

- the Messages relay on 127.0.0.1:<port>, which holds the model credential;
- the robot service (services.controller.frontend --socket), the only robot owner.

Claude Code runs with ``--permission-mode dontAsk`` and an explicit allow list, so
the Read/Edit/Write tools reach only the workspace, and every Bash command runs in
Claude Code's bubblewrap sandbox: writes only in the workspace, no network, the robot
service socket as the only Unix socket, and the repository, robot-controller checkouts,
credentials and the session's private files unreadable. The robot is reachable only
through the MCP tools.

- ``claude-login``: https://api.anthropic.com with the dedicated experiment account's
  long-lived ``claude setup-token`` token (harness/claude_cli/experiment_login.py),
  re-read for every request so a rotated token takes effect at once. The operator's
  personal Claude login (~/.claude) is refused.

summary:
ZED capture service: a separate process that owns the cameras and records them.

Why a separate process: in NEURAL depth mode each ZED keeps a oneTBB pool sized to the
CPU affinity mask spinning for as long as it is open. Unpinned, three of them starved a
PREEMPT_RT kernel and panicked it. The backend therefore starts this server under
`taskset -c <cpus>` with BLAS/OMP thread caps, keeps it free of any libfranka thread, and
the server exits with its parent.

The real scene changes on its own, so every camera streams continuously into a sliding
window the agent can read but not write:

    <stream>/<camera>/<YYYYmmddTHHMM>/<epoch_ms>.jpg          RGB at the stream rate
    <stream>/<camera>/<YYYYmmddTHHMM>/<epoch_ms>_depth.png    depth (uint16 mm) at depth_hz
    <stream>/index.json                                       refreshed every second

Minute directories (UTC) older than the window are deleted as time goes by, once
services.franka.archive has encoded them into the whole-session MP4 archive.

Protocol: one JSON object per line over a private Unix socket.
  {"op": "grab", "cameras": [names], "depth": bool, "out_dir": path}
      -> {"cameras": {name: {"rgb": file, "depth": file|null, "K": 3x3, "width", "height",
                             "timestamp_ns"}}}       (the newest frames, depth on request)
  {"op": "ping"} -> {"open": [names], "frames": {...}, "dropped": {...}}

summary:
Host-side integral outer loop around the Polymetis arm bridge.

The bridge's DROID differential IK re-anchors every command on the measured joints, so
its impedance spring settles short of the goal (about 5 mm in z from an unmodelled
payload, up to 1 cm sideways). This loop sends `goal + bias` and integrates the residual
into the bias, only near the goal or once the arm has stalled, so it does not wind up
while the bridge is still rate-limiting the approach. Verified on the FR3 on 2026-10-03:
10 mm, 3-5 cm and +-15 deg moves settle within 1 mm / 0.5 deg in 1-6 s.

summary:
Gemini (`gemini_generate`) vision helpers: yes / no checks, named points, segmentation masks.

Copy nothing: import this file from your code (see the gemini skill, "Helper module"). Every answer is evidence
for your code, not a decision; geometry (depth, kinematics) stays in your code.

Measured on a robot head camera (2026-10, practice_pnp_box session):
- 640 px wide JPEG (q85, ~35 kB), json_schema, reasoning effort low: 2-6 s, ~$0.004 per call, points within ~6 px
  of depth geometry. A full 1280x720 request timed out after ~65 s and held a large budget reservation.
- max_tokens is shared with reasoning: 2048 truncated a pointing answer; use the 16384 cap, set speed with effort
  ('low' for checks and points, 'minimal' for segmentation, 3-6 s).
- Points and box_2d are [y, x] normalized to 0-1000 over the image sent. Polygon masks came back as [y, x] too,
  even when asked for [x, y]: segment() decides the order per answer by containment in the answer's box_2d.
- The host serializes MCP calls: a pending Gemini call delays robot calls. Ask between motions.
- Reliable for identity, visibility, gross state, points and masks; not for small 3-D changes (lifted / touching):
  measure those with depth. Draw a new prompt's output on the image once before trusting it.

symbols.name: load_image
symbols.doc:
BGR image from an array, an image file, or an observation frame directory (`<camera>.jpg` inside;
`camera` may be omitted when the directory holds one image).

-> (MCP image block, (w, h) of the full-size region the points refer to, (x0, y0) offset of the crop).
crop: (x0, y0, x1, y1) in full-size pixels.

symbols.doc: [y, x] in 0-1000 -> [u, v] full-size pixels.

symbols.name: _call

provider problem: a timeout, refusal, truncation or non-JSON reply is ok False with the reason.

segment

-> {ok, masks: [{label, box_px (u0, v0, u1, v1), poly_px [[u, v], ...]}], mask (uint8 full-size, 1 inside any

summary:
Read the live recording: the robot's cameras and its joint state, last 10 minutes.

The world changes without you: people move objects, things settle or fall, and time
passes while you think. `runtime/stream/` (read-only) always holds the recent past;
`index.json` lists the cameras and their measured frame rates.

    python -m api.stream latest                        # newest frame per camera and its age
    python -m api.stream sheet head_camera --seconds 60 --count 12   # contact sheet -> output/
    python -m api.stream changes head_camera --seconds 300           # when did the scene change?
    python -m api.stream robot --seconds 30                          # joint / end-effector history

Times are epoch milliseconds; file names are the capture times.

summary:
The dedicated Claude account for experiments: its setup-token and identity.

Experiments never use the operator's personal Claude login (~/.claude). A separate
account signs in once in its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and issues a long-lived
``claude setup-token`` token. The relay (messages_relay.Credential) reads only
that token file:

    ~/.config/rax/                       (0700; RAX_CLAUDE_EXPERIMENT_DIR overrides)
      claude-experiment-home/            dedicated CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, for sign-in only
      claude-experiment.token            the token (0600), re-read by the relay per request
      claude-experiment.json             identity (0600): email, organization, created_at

Set up or rotate with ``bash scripts/setup_claude_experiment_login.sh``. With
``--personal`` the operator deliberately bills their own signed-in account instead: the
token is issued from the default login and recorded as ``personal: true``, which turns
off the personal-account refusal for that token only.

summary:
Run Claude Code on the host as the robot agent, separated from the robot infrastructure.

The launcher (trusted, operator-run) prepares a session under the artifact root:

    <session>/
      configuration.json     operator configuration (services.controller.config)
      model-relay.json       provider, models and the credential *path* (never the token)
      agent-workspace/       the agent's cwd and its only writable directory
      claude-home/           CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and HOME of the agent: settings.json, mcp.json
      state.json, mcp.jsonl  robot-service ledger and audit log (unreadable to the agent)
      agent-lifecycle.json   launches, usage waits and exit status

and per launch starts two host services the agent cannot read or modify:

- the Messages relay on 127.0.0.1:<port>, which holds the model credential;
- the robot service (services.controller.frontend --socket), the only robot owner.

Claude Code runs with ``--permission-mode dontAsk`` and an explicit allow list, so
the Read/Edit/Write tools reach only the workspace, and every Bash command runs in
Claude Code's bubblewrap sandbox: writes only in the workspace, internet only through the
sandbox proxy (which refuses the robot controller), the host sockets that would bypass the
robot service hidden, and the repository, credentials, the operator's RAX_PROTECTED_PATHS
(robot-controller checkouts, SDK environments) and the session's private files unreadable.
The robot is reachable only through the MCP tools.

summary:
Stdio MCP server for Claude Code that forwards to the session's robot service socket.

Claude Code spawns this as its MCP server; the robot service (services.controller.frontend
--socket) is started once by the launcher and owns the robot, so Claude Code's direct
tool calls and the agent's Python scripts share one serialized robot owner.

Host-only Anthropic Messages endpoint for Claude Code. The agent never holds credentials.

The host-run Claude Code talks to ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:<port> (this
relay, on loopback TCP; a Unix socket path is also accepted). The relay adds the
provider credential and enforces a model allowlist, a model-call cap, local
(client-executed) tools only, inline media only, bounded bodies, and provider
throttling retried before any byte reaches the client. Token usage is appended to a
host-side JSONL for the operator.

Providers:
- ``openrouter``: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/messages with the OpenRouter key.
- ``anthropic``: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with an API key (x-api-key).
- ``claude-login``: https://api.anthropic.com with the dedicated experiment account's
  long-lived ``claude setup-token`` token (harness/claude_cli/experiment_login.py),
  re-read for every request so a rotated token takes effect at once. The operator's
  personal Claude login (~/.claude) is refused.

summary:
Write a new session configuration under the artifact root; starts nothing.

python scripts/configure_session.py --task stack_cups --task-file task.md [--robot rby1]
bash scripts/start_agent.sh --config <printed path>

Characterize the RB-Y1 backend's control tools on the robot (docs/REAL_ROBOT_ADAPTATION.md, Rule 2).

    $PY scripts/rby1_characterize.py <session_root> <part> [<part> ...]

Runs through the real Rby1Backend (the agent's guards), with the operator's arming and a
person at the e-stop. Every move is small, starts from the current pose (normally `ready`)
and returns to it. Results are printed and saved as JSON under
<artifact root>/characterization/<UTC stamp>_<part>.json, to be summarized in RBY1.md and
the control skills.

Parts:
  overhead    wall time of rby1_status, rby1_observe and a 0.01 rad head move (calls only)
  refusals    the exact refusal text at each limit (validation only: nothing moves)
  joints      duration and final error by move size, small to normal (up to 1 rad): head tilt and
              pan, arm wrist, arm elbow, torso yaw, torso height (upright rule kept); and the same
              arm move with the controller's hold time 1.0 s vs 0.2 s
  repeat      the right hand to the same +5 cm pose 5 times from `ready`: spread of the
              reached positions (rby1_move_eef)
  eef         rby1_move_eef 2 / 5 / 10 / 20 cm along x, y, z on the right arm: final error,
              duration, and the deviation of the hand's path (FK of the measured joints,
              sampled during the move) from the straight line
  look        rby1_look_at a few points: predicted vs. reached pointing error
  gripper     open / close duration and openings at two current limits (no object)
  observe     depth validity, intrinsics, stream rates, and pixel_to_position repeatability
              of one image point over 3 frames
  base        forward 0.3 m and back, turn +-0.5 rad (0.1 m/s, 0.2 rad/s): odometry against
              the depth-measured distance to a fixed point straight ahead
              (base_line: only the straight moves; base_turn: only the turns)

symbols.doc: Median depth-measured distance to the scene straight ahead (a patch at the image centre).

summary:
Operator-supervised characterization of the controller's own command modes (controller_modes.py).

    $PY scripts/rby1_controller_check.py <session_root> [part ...]

The session must be configured with backend option controller_commands = true. One arming
covers the run (`rby1 arm`, a person at the e-stop). Every move goes through the real backend
and its guards, starts from `ready` and is small (a few centimetres in free space in front of
the robot); each part ends back at `ready`. Per move it records the duration, the final
position error, the deviation of the hand path from the straight line, how much each part
moved (torso use), torso roll (torso_0 / torso_4), the peak joint load and any guard stop.
Results: runtime/characterization/controller_check_*.json.

Parts (default: all, in this order):
  ready      rest -> half -> ready (joint space, as before)
  optimal    rby1_optimal_control, body: right hand +5 cm forward, back; left hand +5 cm up,
             back; both hands +4 cm forward together, back; right hand 10 cm down (the torso
             may join), back
  cartesian  rby1_cartesian: right_arm +5 cm forward and back, +0.3 rad about the hand's own
             axis and back; body: left hand +5 cm sideways and back
  eef        rby1_move_eef in controller mode: right hand +3 cm up and back
  impedance  rby1_cartesian_impedance right +3 cm and back; rby1_link_impedance left hold
             +2 cm for 3 s; rby1_joint_impedance right wrist +0.1 rad and back
  jog        rby1_jog right_arm_6 +0.1 / -0.1, head_0 +0.1 / -0.1; rby1_joint_group torso_5
             +0.1 and back
  stop       rby1_hold mode stop_command while idle (the StopCommand path)

symbols.name: run
symbols.doc: One tool call with 25 Hz sampling; returns the reply, or None after a handled stop (recorded).

summary:
Operator-supervised health check of the RB-Y1 through the real Rby1Backend, at its slow defaults.

    $PY scripts/configure_session.py --task health_check --task-text "health check" --robot rby1
    $PY scripts/rby1_health_check.py <session_root> [part ...]

One arming covers the whole run (`rby1 arm 30`, a person at the e-stop). Every move goes
through the agent's tools and guards, while a sampler records joint position, velocity,
torque and drive temperature at 25 Hz. Per move it prints the duration, the final error,
the peak velocity and acceleration (smoothness) and the highest torque as a fraction of
the joint's rating. Raw samples and results go to runtime/characterization/health_*.json.

Parts (default: all, in this order):
  rest      no motion: faults, temperatures, holding torque vs the vendor gravity model
  ready     torso, arms and head to `ready` / `zero` (one rby1_move_body)
  joints    each arm joint 0.1 rad out and back, torso squat +-0.1 rad (torso_1, torso_2 = -2x),
            torso_3 lean +0.05, torso_5 yaw +-0.1, head pan / tilt +-0.15
  sweep     a larger, slow arm move (shoulder 0.5 rad out and back) for the velocity profile
  guards    the new guards on the hardware, none of which can push anything: (1) with the
            right shoulder's rating lowered so that its guard sits 4 N m above its starting
            load, a shoulder lift that raises the load is stopped and the joints are
            re-targeted where they stopped; (2) the watchdog with its guard set
            below the standing load re-targets in place (must move < 2 mrad); (3) a
            0.01 mrad "exact" tolerance makes a normal move count as blocked: the in-place
            re-target after a finished command must not move the arm
  gripper   close and open each gripper (homes both first)
  restore   back to the pose the run started from
  base      (only when named) forward 0.1 m and back, turn +-0.2 rad at the new caps: clear
            the floor around the base first

symbols.name: Sampler
symbols.doc: Joint state at 25 Hz while a backend call runs in this thread's caller.

summary:
Operator-supervised large-motion test of the RB-Y1: squats, arm stretches, long hand paths.

    $PY scripts/rby1_large_motion.py <session_root> [part ...]

Everything goes through the agent's tools and guards (limits, squat cap, self-collision,
gravity load, torque guard, in-place re-target) at the backend's slow defaults, from the
`ready` posture and back to it, one arm at a time. Moves larger than 1.0 rad on a joint are
split into chained calls. A refusal by the backend is recorded and the part goes on with
the next posture (refusals are results too). Joint state is sampled at 25 Hz as in
rby1_health_check.py; results go to runtime/characterization/large_motion_*.json.

Parts (default: all, in this order):
  clearance  head camera at pan -0.47 / 0 / +0.47: depth points (not the robot itself, not
             the floor) inside 1.0 m of the base, per zone; refuses to go on if anything is
             inside the arms' reach (0.95 m) unless --ignore-clearance; frames are saved
  squat      torso ready -> 45 -> 60 -> 69 deg (the cap) -> back to ready with the arms in ready,
             then a forward lean at ready (torso_3 +0.15)
  lean       at each torso height (zero, ready, mid, low, lowest): lean +0.10 and +0.15, and at
             +0.15 each hand 0.08 m forward and back (rby1_move_eef); then arms `park` at
             `mid` with lean +0.2 and +0.3
  stretch    each arm: forward horizontal, forward-up 45 deg, overhead, back; forward-out
             45 deg, sideways 60 deg, back; forearm roll +-1.0, wrist roll +-1.2; then both
             arms forward together (these are the arm presets forward, forward_up, overhead,
             forward_out and side)
  reach      right hand through a 0.2 m square in front of the shoulder and a 0.25 m reach
             forward with rby1_move_eef, path deviation from the straight line measured
  low        squat 60 deg + right hand forward-down to table height, a 0.1 m descent there
             with rby1_move_eef, and back
  restore    back to the pose the run started from

symbols.name: run
symbols.doc: One call with sampling; a backend refusal (ValueError) is recorded and returned as None.

symbols.name: body
symbols.doc: rby1_move_body to {component: positions}, split so no joint moves more than MAX_CHUNK_RAD per call.

symbols.name: clearance
symbols.doc: Depth points inside REACH_M + 0.05 of the base, excluding the robot (FK link origins) and the floor.

summary:
Operator-supervised motion check through the real Rby1Backend (same guards the agent gets).

    $PY scripts/configure_session.py --task motion_check --task-text "motion check" --robot rby1
    $PY scripts/rby1_motion_check.py <session_root> <step>

It connects, waits up to 5 minutes for the operator to arm the session (`rby1 arm 5`, a
person at the e-stop), runs one step and closes. Every move is small and returns to the
pose the step started from; a move that does not arrive stops the step. Nothing moves
before the operator arms; the first armed step powers the drives on (they then hold).
Run each step once with nothing near the robot and record the printed numbers in
RBY1.md "Motion check". Re-run after any firmware or rby1_sdk upgrade.

Steps:
  status       connect and print status (no arming, nothing moves, nothing is powered)
  disarmed     motion refused while disarmed (moves nothing)
  head         head pan +0.1 rad and back, tilt +0.1 rad and back
  wrists       both arms' last joint +0.1 rad and back
  joints_all   every arm joint by 0.05 / 0.1 rad, direction chosen by FK to move the hand
               away from the body; all back
  torso        torso_5 (chest yaw) +0.05 rad and back; torso_3 (lean) +0.05 rad and back
  body         torso and both arms to `half`, then `ready`, head to `zero` (two rby1_move_body
               calls); the starting pose is NOT restored (`ready` is the neutral pose)
  base         forward / back 5 cm at 0.05 m/s, turn +-0.1 rad at 0.1 rad/s (wheel odometry)
  ik           each arm's end effector up 2 cm and back, forward 2 cm and back (rby1_move_eef)
  gripper      home both grippers (each is pushed fully closed, then fully open), then close and
               open each fully through rby1_gripper
  disarm_test  head tilt towards +0.3 rad at 0.1 rad/s; `rby1 disarm` mid-motion must stop it
               (PASS = cancelled, stopped short, then held within 0.005 rad from 0.5 s to 3 s)
  disarm_arm   the same with the right elbow (right_arm_3) +0.5 rad at the arms' normal 0.3 rad/s

symbols.name: disarm_test
symbols.doc: Disarm mid-motion: one joint of one component moves by delta; disarm once it has moved 0.05 rad.

symbols.name: outward_sign
symbols.doc: +1 or -1: the direction of this arm joint that moves the hand away from the body midline (|y| up).

summary:
Derive a standard-URDF copy of the RB-Y1 vendor model for generic tools (pinocchio, yourdfpy, trimesh).

    python scripts/standardize_urdf.py <vendor model.urdf> <out.urdf>

The vendor file (rby1-sdk models/rby1a/urdf) uses two things standard URDF parsers reject:
`<capsule radius= length=>` collision geometry and wheel `<limit>` without `effort`. The
copy replaces each capsule (axis z of its origin) with the identical union of a cylinder and
two end spheres, and gives the wheel limits effort="0". Visual meshes, inertias, joints and
limits are unchanged. The vendor files stay as shipped; this only writes a new file.
Trusted robot service, robot backends and operator tools.

Whole-session archive of the live stream: one H.264 MP4 per camera per minute.

The live stream (services/rby1/recorder.py) keeps only a sliding window. As each minute completes,
this archiver encodes its JPEG frames into

    <archive>/<camera>/<UTC YYYYmmddTHHMM>.mp4    H.264, nominal stream fps
    <archive>/<camera>/<UTC YYYYmmddTHHMM>.json   exact capture time of every frame (epoch ms)
    <archive>/robot/<UTC YYYYmmddTHHMM>.jsonl     the arm/gripper log of that minute

so the session can be replayed in sync with the agent's transcript and tool log (all
epoch-timestamped). Frame k of an MP4 is `frames_ms[k]` in its sidecar; playback at the
nominal fps is only approximately real time. Depth is not archived (~10 GB/hour).

Operator motion arming: a file in the session root that only the operator writes.

The agent's sandbox cannot write outside its workspace, so it cannot arm itself. The
backend re-reads the file before and during every motion; disarming stops a running
motion within one servo period.

summary:
Robot backends behind the agent MCP. The frontend never imports a backend directly.

A backend is constructed once per session by the frontend process (the only robot
owner) and implements:

    tools() -> list[dict]            MCP tool definitions (name, description, inputSchema)
    call(name, arguments) -> (value, images)
                                     value: JSON-safe dict; images: MCP image content
                                     blocks {'type': 'image', 'mimeType', 'data'(base64)}
    status() -> dict                 live robot summary merged into the `status` tool
    close()                          release hardware; must be safe to call twice

Optional: ``mutating`` (set of tool names that can move hardware; a failure in one
marks control uncertain) and ``validate(name, arguments)`` (raise before any motion).

A robot may also register read-only telemetry for the operator dashboard: a class whose
``snapshot()`` returns a JSON-safe dict with ``kind`` and ``ok``. It must never command
the robot, since it runs next to a session's backend.

Trusted, MCP-only execution backend for autonomous robot controllers.

Nothing in this package is mounted into untrusted containers except runtime.py.
The existing interactive launchers are deliberately not changed by this backend.
Host-only Gemini dollar accounting. Integer nanodollars avoid float drift.
Operator-owned session configuration. No values are accepted from agent code.

Host-owned robot/API MCP server: the agent's only path to the robot and to Gemini.

agent CLI's stdio bridge (harness/claude_cli/mcp_bridge.py) and the agent's own
Python scripts (auto_research_agent/api/runtime.py); every call runs on one
dispatcher thread, so two clients never drive the robot at once. Without --socket it

summary: A hardware-free backend for tests and launcher dry runs. It moves nothing.

MCP backend for the real Rainbow Robotics RB-Y1 (model A) through rby1_sdk.

The robot's controller (192.168.30.1:50051, gRPC) runs the joint and wheel controllers;
this process runs on the robot's UPC (a Jetson) and talks to it with rby1_sdk 0.8.3
(`services.rby1.robot`, the only module that sends robot commands). Body: a
differential-drive base, a 6-joint torso, two 7-DoF arms with two-finger Dynamixel
grippers on the UPC's USB bus, and a 2-joint head carrying a ZED 2i stereo camera.

Safety layering, outermost first:
  1. The physical emergency stop and the operator beside the robot. The backend also
     reads the EMO state and refuses or stops motion while one is pressed.
  2. Operator arming (services.arming): motion tools refuse unless armed, and a running
     motion stops within one control period once the operator disarms.
  3. This backend: joint targets inside the URDF limits minus a margin, per-call joint and
     base displacement caps, slow joint and base speeds with gentle acceleration, an upright
     torso rule and a squat limit, end-effector height, self-collision (vendor
     collision model) and the gravity load on every joint (vendor dynamics) checked along
     the whole joint path, and a wrist-force guard while the arms move. Joint moves are
     timed position commands on the robot's controller, polled at control_hz; disarming,
     the EMO, stale state, a drive that is not ready, no progress, a force spike or a joint
     torque over 150 % of its rating cancels the motion and holds.
     A joint left short of its target (an end stop, a contact) is re-targeted to where it is:
     otherwise its drive winds up to its current limit and faults, and every joint drops
     (that happened on the robot). A watchdog does the same between calls.
     Connecting moves nothing and changes no robot state: power, servo and the control
     manager come up at the first armed motion, and the drives then hold where they are.
     A controller fault disarms the session and is reset only after the operator arms again.
  4. The robot controller's own limits and faults.

symbols.name: _fresh
symbols.doc: Raise MotionStopped unless every joint of the components ('wheels' too) reported recently.

symbols.name: _require_armed
symbols.doc:
Arming, a released EMO and no unacknowledged fault, then power / servo / control manager up,
cool drives and a fresh state.

symbols.name: _enable
symbols.doc:
Power, servo and control manager on (the vendor's order), checked before every armed motion.

Idempotent: it acts only on what is off, so after an emergency stop (which drops power
and faults the control manager) the next motion the operator arms brings them back. A
fault is reset only when the operator armed after the backend disarmed for it.
Moves nothing: the drives then hold where they are.

symbols.name: _disarm
symbols.doc: The backend disarms the session (EMO, controller fault, drive not ready): the operator re-arms on purpose.

symbols.name: _check_path
symbols.doc: Per-call step cap, then end-effector height and self-collision along the joint paths moved together.

symbols.name: _look_at_goal
symbols.doc: Head pan / tilt that point the head camera's optical axis at a base-frame point.

symbols.name: _drive_posture
symbols.doc: Refuse driving with the body low, leaning or stretched out (the base can tip or sweep things).

symbols.name: _plan
symbols.doc:
The joint goals a motion tool would command from q, after every planning check the tool makes
before moving ({} for the base). ValueError names the refusal.

symbols.name: _check_arguments
symbols.doc: Refuse argument keys a tool does not define (top level and nested objects), instead of ignoring them.

symbols.name: _guard
symbols.doc: Every control period of a motion: arming, EMO, fresh joint state, wrist force; the snapshot.

symbols.name: _over_torque
symbols.doc:
{joint: 'tau N m (fraction of rated)'} of joints whose measured torque is over the guard.

With a baseline (the torques when the motion started), a joint that was already over the guard
then counts only once it rises a further torque_rise_fraction of its rating: a motion that holds
or eases a load (backing off, setting an object down) is never blocked by that load.

symbols.name: _relieve
symbols.doc:
Re-target the torso and arms to where they are now: a zero-length move.

A joint held short of its target (an end stop, a contact) keeps pushing until its drive
faults; a target at the measured position ends the push. Waits for the cancel of any
running command and for the joints to slow first, so the new target is where they stop.

symbols.name: _retarget_here
symbols.doc:
Cancel running commands, let the joints slow, then a joint-position target at the measured pose.

Returns (snapshot before, snapshot after); the move is zero-length by construction.

symbols.name: _held
symbols.doc: Mark a handled stop: everything holds at a measured state, nothing else is pending.

symbols.name: _failed
symbols.doc:
An unexpected exception during a motion (an SDK or driver error): hold, attach the measured
state, and let the original exception through unchanged so the agent sees its type, message
and traceback.

symbols.name: _duration
symbols.doc: Time of a trapezoidal (or triangular) velocity profile over step at that component's caps.

symbols.name: _run
symbols.doc:
Joint targets for one or more components as one timed command on the robot's controller.

Every control period re-checks arming, the EMO, state freshness and (for arm and torso
moves) the wrist forces; a component that makes no progress, a deadline, or a
controller finish code other than Ok cancels the command and holds.

symbols.name: _blocked
symbols.doc: {joint: shortfall rad} of torso / arm joints still off their target after exact_timeout_s.

symbols.name: _hypothetical
symbols.doc: q with components replaced as in rby1_move_body targets, without the limit checks (reported instead).

symbols.name: _body_report
symbols.doc: Hands, collisions, limits and gravity load of a posture.

symbols.name: _watch_once
symbols.doc: Faults and drives not ready disarm the session; a joint pushing over its rating is re-targeted.

symbols.name: _robot_record
symbols.doc: The recorder's robot state record: joints, end-effector positions, odometry, wrist forces.

symbols.name: _sensor_status
symbols.doc: Which perception sources are delivering now.

The RB-Y1 head camera (ZED 2i stereo, USB on the robot's UPC) through the ZED SDK (pyzed).

One grab thread keeps the newest left RGB image (and depth) with its capture time; the
backend's observations and the live recording both read that latest frame, so the camera
is opened once per robot service. Only one process can open a ZED: stop any other ZED
publisher on the UPC before a session.

symbols.doc:
A frame that shows nothing: one flat colour, or the solid green (R = B = 0) the ZED SDK delivered
after its own "successful" recovery from a USB connection failure (2026-10-09, push_chair session).

symbols.doc: Never serve an empty frame; reopen the camera when they persist.

symbols.name: read
symbols.doc: (capture time s, rgb, depth m or None) of the newest frame, or None before the first.

summary:
The RB-Y1 controller's own command modes as MCP tools: wired, not reimplemented.

Each tool maps its arguments onto one rby1_sdk command builder, used as shipped
(`SdkRobot.controller_command`): Cartesian (CartesianCommandBuilder), whole-body optimal
control (OptimalControlCommandBuilder), Cartesian impedance
(CartesianImpedanceControlCommandBuilder), link impedance (ImpedanceControlCommandBuilder),
joint impedance (JointImpedanceControlCommandBuilder), torso joint group
(JointGroupPositionCommandBuilder), jog (JogCommandBuilder) and the stop command
(StopCommandBuilder). The robot's controller solves the IK and the path; the backend
solves nothing itself.

The agent chooses what to do (mode, targets, a speed below the cap), never how the
controller behaves: impedance gains, torque limits and solver settings (stop costs,
patience, scaling, tracking tolerances) are backend options from the vendor examples,
set by the operator. Nothing here writes a robot parameter, and gravity compensation is
not wired.

Because the controller picks the joint path, the checks before a command are on its
targets (height, travel, reach, joint limits) and the checks while it runs are on the
measured state every control period: arming, EMO, fresh state, drives ready, torque and
wrist force (`_guard`), and an envelope (joints moving towards a limit, the squat cap, the
upright torso, end-effector height, new self-collisions). A command ends with the joints
re-targeted where they are, so whatever the controller holds afterwards is a joint hold
at the measured position.

Characterized on the robot on 2026-10-08 (scripts/rby1_controller_check.py, RBY1.md) and on
by default (`controller_commands`); `controller_tools_disabled` lists the modes that failed
there: link impedance with the vendor's gains overloaded the wrist (202 % of its rating in
1.3 s) and Cartesian impedance ended 66 mm from a 3 cm target. Re-enabling them means new
gains (operator options) and a new characterization.

symbols.name: ControllerModes
symbols.doc: Mixin for Rby1Backend: tool definitions, checks and supervised execution of the controller modes.

symbols.name: _resolve_target
symbols.doc: Base-frame 4x4 target for one link, after the boundary checks.

symbols.name: _controller_plan
symbols.doc: (kind, component, spec, moving components, summary) of a controller-mode call; ValueError if refused.

symbols.name: _envelope
symbols.doc: MotionStopped if the measured state leaves the envelope while the controller drives it.

symbols.name: _supervise
symbols.doc: Watch a controller command every control period until it finishes (or for `seconds`).

summary:
The RB-Y1 two-finger grippers: two Dynamixels on the UPC's local USB bus, via rby1_sdk.

`rby1_sdk.upc.GripperDeviceName` (/dev/rby1_gripper), protocol 2.0 at 2 Mbaud, ID 0 the
right gripper and ID 1 the left, powered by the arms' tool flanges at 12 V. This follows
the SDK's teleoperation example (examples/python/17_teleoperation_with_joint_mapping.py).

Nothing moves until `home()`: it powers the flanges, then sweeps both grippers to their
two ends under a small current to find the encoder range, which MOVES the fingers. After
that a background loop holds both at their targets in current-based position mode, where
the current limit is the grip force. Only one process can own the bus.

symbols.name: home
symbols.doc:
Power the flanges, find both encoder ranges by a slow sweep (moves the fingers), then hold.

guard() is called every tick and may raise to abort; the fingers then go limp.

symbols.name: command
symbols.doc: Set a target opening (m, 0 = closed) and current limit (A) for one gripper.

symbols.name: hold
symbols.doc: Keep each gripper where it is now (target = measured).

symbols.name: widths
symbols.doc: {side: measured opening in m, or None}.

Frames are the robot's `base` frame: x forward, y left, z up, metres. The joint vector is
the SDK's 24-vector in `Model_A.robot_joint_names` order (two wheels, six torso joints,
right arm, left arm, two head joints). The head camera's optical frame (z forward, x
right, y down) is `link_head_2` composed with a hand-eye calibration (X_HEAD_CAMERA by default),
so pixel back-projection composes with `frame(HEAD_CAMERA, q)` directly.

symbols.name: with_component
symbols.doc: A copy of the 24-vector q with one component replaced.

symbols.doc:
Forward kinematics, a damped least-squares arm IK and self-collision on the vendor model.

Give the robot's own URDF text (`Robot.get_robot_model()`, matching its firmware) or a

capture_once

summary:
The thin live half of the RB-Y1 backend: the only module that calls rby1_sdk's robot API.

It connects to the robot's controller over gRPC (`rby1_sdk.create_robot_a`, firmware/SDK
0.8.3 on this robot) and offers the backend a small surface: a state snapshot, bringing
power / servo / control manager up (a controller fault is reset only when the caller says
the operator allowed it), timed joint-position commands, and a base velocity stream. Everything in it is a plain call of the SDK's public API: no vendor
code is patched, and no robot parameter is written (`set_parameter` is never called).

SDK facts it relies on (rby1_sdk 0.8.3):
- `connect()` only opens the gRPC channel: it changes no power, servo or control state.
- Dropping a command handler or stream cancels its command (their destructors call
  Cancel), so every handler that must keep running is kept on this object.
- Cancelling a command stops the joints with the controller's own deceleration, and the
  drives then hold where they stopped.
- A finished joint-position command leaves the joints holding at its target. A joint that
  cannot reach that target (an end stop, a contact) keeps pushing: the drive's integral
  term winds up to its current limit and the drive faults (seen on the robot: torso_2 at
  2.6 x its rated torque for 1.2 s, then a MajorFault and every joint dropped).

symbols.name: Snapshot
symbols.doc: One robot state read; every array is in Model_A.robot_joint_names order.

symbols.name: Handle
symbols.doc: A sent command: kept alive here so that the SDK does not cancel it.

symbols.name: BaseStream
symbols.doc: An SE(2) velocity command stream; silence (no send within hold_s) stops the base.

symbols.name: finish
symbols.doc: The finish code name once done ('Ok', 'Canceled', 'Preempted', ...).

symbols.name: wait
symbols.doc: True once the command is done (finished or cancelled), waiting at most timeout_ms.

symbols.name: send
symbols.doc:
Send one velocity. A stream the controller expired underneath us (a late cancel of the previous
control, seen right after a previous base move) is replaced and the send repeated, at most
MAX_RENEWALS times per stream; the caller's loop closes on odometry, so continuing is safe.

symbols.name: close
symbols.doc:
Zero velocity, then let the hold time end the stream; cancel only if it is still running.

The SDK's cancel cancels the robot's current control, and it can land after the next command has
started (a base move sent 10-30 ms after the previous one failed with "This stream is expired").
Ending by the hold time cancels nothing.

symbols.name: control_state
symbols.doc: {'power': bool, 'servo': bool, 'manager': 'Idle'|'Enabled'|'MinorFault'|..., 'control': ...}.

symbols.name: manager_state
symbols.doc: The control manager state name alone ('Enabled', 'Idle', 'MinorFault', 'MajorFault', ...).

symbols.name: enable
symbols.doc:
Power, servo and control manager on, in the vendor's order; returns the steps taken.

A faulted control manager is reset only with reset_faults (the operator armed after
seeing the fault); otherwise RuntimeError. The drives then hold the joints where they
are; no motion command is sent.

symbols.name: joint_command
symbols.doc: One RobotCommandBuilder that moves the given components ({component: goal}) together.

symbols.name: stop
symbols.doc:
Cancel every live command and wait until each cancel is done; returns how many were running.

The controller then decelerates the joints and holds them where they stop (on the robot:
0.04 rad past the cancel at 0.3 rad/s, then within 0.0001 rad over 3 s). No hold command
is sent: the SDK's cancel cancels the robot's current control, which took a hold sent
after it with it, and an accepted hold at the pre-deceleration position would pull the
joints back, a motion after a stop.

symbols.name: controller_command
symbols.doc:
Send one of the controller's command modes for a component; returns a Handle.

kind: 'cartesian' (CartesianCommandBuilder), 'optimal_control' (OptimalControlCommandBuilder),
'cartesian_impedance' (CartesianImpedanceControlCommandBuilder), 'link_impedance'
(ImpedanceControlCommandBuilder), 'joint_impedance' (JointImpedanceControlCommandBuilder),
'joint_group' (JointGroupPositionCommandBuilder, torso), 'jog' (JogCommandBuilder, one joint),
'stop' (StopCommandBuilder). spec holds plain values (lists, floats, 4x4 lists); this method only
maps them onto the builder calls. component: right_arm, left_arm, torso or body (jog / stop: None).

symbols.name: _wrap

summary:

Its own gRPC connection to the robot's controller that only reads (`get_state`,
`get_control_manager_state`, `is_power_on`): never a command, never a power, servo or
parameter call, so it is safe next to a running session's robot service.

Zip finished sessions and ship them off the robot so its disk never fills.

The launcher starts this after every run (`--session <root> --sweep`); it can also be run
by hand. For each finished session:

  1. zip it into <artifact root>/outbox/<session>__<status>__<UTC stamp>.zip (media stored,
     everything else deflated) with a .sha256 next to it;
  2. rsync the zip to RAX_SHIP_DEST (scp-style `host:/dir`; there is no default, and
     without it nothing ships) and verify the remote sha256 over ssh;
  3. only after a verified copy: delete the local zip, write <session>/.shipped.json, and
     delete the session directory. A run that was interrupted (status `stopped`) stays
     on disk so `start_agent.sh --resume` still works; it ships again when it ends.

`--sweep` retries every finished session that has not been shipped since it last
changed, then, while free space is below RAX_SHIP_MIN_FREE_GB, deletes the oldest
sessions that are already shipped and unchanged since.

    python -m services.runtime_ship --session <root> [--sweep] [--dry-run]
    python -m services.runtime_ship --sweep

summary:
The agent's persistent skill library: task skills learned across sessions, one git repository per robot.

Separate from the harness's read-only skills (`agent_skills/`, rendered into `.agents/skills/`):
those are written by people; this library is written by agents, one session at a time.

    <artifact root>/skill-library/<robot>/      the library (git, branch main); only the harness writes it
    <session>/agent-workspace/skill-library/    the session's clone, on branch session/<session name>

The agent reads the library, runs its skills, and commits new or improved skills on its
session branch. `merge()` (the harness tool `skill_library_merge`) validates the branch and
merges it into main. The harness never runs git inside the agent's clone (its config and
hooks are the agent's): it copies the clone's object store to a scratch directory with a
fresh config and no hooks, fetches the branch from there into the library, validates the
files of that commit as data (code is only compiled, never run), and merges.

Format (enforced by `validate_tree`, documented in the library README and the agent's
`continual-learning` skill):

    INDEX.md                         one table row per skill: slug link, status, what, when
    skills/<slug>/SKILL.md           frontmatter + the required sections below
    skills/<slug>/code/*.py          the executable procedure; the entry defines main(ctx, ...)
    skills/<slug>/evidence/runs.jsonl  one JSON object per run of the code
    skills/<slug>/evidence/images/   visual references (jpg / png) the runs and SKILL.md cite

- a detailed operator-side review (Gemini, the session's review ledger) from the simulator's
  goal report, the code's tool calls and log, and those frames;

layout it plays. Host records: ``<session>/code-run-reports/layout-NNN/`` holds ``replay/``,

summary:
BEHAVIOR-1K (OmniGibson, R1Pro) simulator backend for the auto-research harness.

imported solely by ``server.py`` and ``session.py``, which run in the separate

Reviews of finished BEHAVIOR exploration episodes from the simulator's ground truth.

Operator-side, stdlib + numpy only. The simulator writes ``sim/private_goal_report.json``
(every grounded goal condition with its initial and final truth, and the extents of the
objects involved). This module classifies the conditions, describes each missed one in
relative geometry, and asks Gemini for a short explanation using that report, the
episode's tool trace and its final frames.

Two outputs: the full operator record (report, explanation, cost), and the agent-facing
review. A standard review is the analyst's explanation alone and carries no scores. A
detailed review adds the episode's partial score and the ground-truth goal checklist with
its geometry, and the analyst may quote exact numbers. Either names objects only by their
task names (``detergent bottle 1``) and carries no scene names or world coordinates.
Formal episodes are never reviewed live; a finished code-mode session's runs of its own code
are reviewed for its later live copies (``services/agent_formal/code_runs.py``), from the
code's log as well.

symbols.doc: Signed horizontal distance (m) from ``point`` to the box's xy footprint edge: positive inside.

symbols.name: _gap
symbols.doc: Per-axis separation between two boxes (m); 0 where they overlap.

symbols.doc: Collision links of a fixed object whose footprint contains ``point``, with their bottom height.

symbols.name: posture

symbols.doc: One line of relative geometry for a binary relation between task objects ``a`` and ``b``.

summary:
cuRobo free-space arm planning inside the OmniGibson process (runs in runtime/envs/behavior).

Challenge-compliant: the planner's world collision checker is created empty and never
updated (``skip_obstacle_update=True``), so it avoids self-collision only and never reads
scene meshes. Targets arrive in the robot base frame (the frame of the proprioceptive EEF
poses). The wrapper plans relative to the holonomic base's virtual root link and refreshes
the locked joints (virtual base, and the trunk for ``arm_no_torso``) from the current state,
so targets are converted to world coordinates here, inside the simulator; the world pose
never leaves this process. Plans become native 23-D rows at the control rate and run
through the ordinary episode step path.

symbols.name: generator
symbols.doc:
cuRobo's ARM embodiment (trunk and both arms) or its arms-only variant (trunk locked
at its current joints by the wrapper's per-plan locked-joint refresh).

On sm_120 GPUs the arms-only variant's finetune trajopt would launch cuRobo's fused
L-BFGS kernel (history 27) with 392 threads x 168 registers, over the per-block
register limit ("too many resources requested for launch"; NVlabs/curobo#716). The
trunk-enabled variant already uses cuRobo's PyTorch L-BFGS step there, so the
arms-only finetune solver is configured the same way.

symbols.name: release
symbols.doc: Free the current generator, its CUDA graphs and their memory pools.

symbols.name: _rows
symbols.doc: Full-robot joint waypoints (at the sim step) -> 23-D rows at the control rate.

symbols.name: eef_move
symbols.doc:
Closed-loop damped least-squares IK for one arm toward a robot-base-frame pose: the
trunk, base and other arm hold their measured joints. Uses the robot's relative
Jacobian (base-body frame) each control step. Local and not collision-aware, like
RoboDojo's EEF stepping.

symbols.name: _store
symbols.doc: Keep only the newest preview plan; the ones it replaces say so when used.

symbols.name: plan_rows
symbols.doc: A cached plan's native rows, for the robot-only preview; the plan stays executable.

Host-side owner of the BEHAVIOR robot-only preview process (stdlib + msgpack + numpy only).

One persistent ``python -m services.behavior.preview_server`` per backend, started on the
first preview run and reused until the backend closes. It holds an R1Pro on a floor
plane with fixed third-person cameras; it never sees a live episode.

BEHAVIOR robot-only motion preview service: ``python -m services.behavior.preview_server``.

Runs in runtime/envs/behavior. One persistent process serves any number of preview runs
over the same msgpack RPC as the episode simulator.

Robot-only BEHAVIOR motion preview inside OmniGibson (runs in runtime/envs/behavior).

The R1Pro of the official evaluation (``omnigibson/eval/r1pro.yaml``: controllers, base
mass, 30 Hz actions over 120 Hz physics) stands alone on a floor plane, watched by fixed
third-person cameras. Each run starts from the joint state the caller supplies, executes
native 23-D rows exactly as an episode would, and returns third-person frames and the
measured end state. There is no scene, object or task: nothing here reads a live episode.

with only proprioception: the preview shows third-person views, not the robot cameras.

symbols.name: run
symbols.doc:
``measured``: the start state is the live episode's measured joints, not caller input,
so joint drift past a limit is clamped and reported like any measured hold.

symbols.name: simulator_environment

symbols.name: BehaviorProcess
symbols.doc: One simulator process, its RPC client and its identity-checked requests.

Runs only in ``runtime/envs/behavior``, like ``server.py``. It resets the episode's task
instance under the same evaluator configuration, steps every recorded
``<episode>/action_NNNNNN.json`` row in order, and saves the head and wrist RGB frames at the
requested steps and at the end. Physics need not repeat exactly, so every replayed base pose
is compared with the run's recorded one (``private_base_truth.jsonl``), and the replay's final
goal conditions with the run's goal report. ``replay.json`` records both comparisons and the
saved frames.

summary:
Background reviews of finished BEHAVIOR exploration episodes (operator-side).

Reviews are part of closing an episode: the session's episode management (the supervisor
for single-environment episodes and rehearsals, the exploration pool for parallel ones)
reports each closed episode to the session's ``EpisodeReviews``, owned by its MCP service
(``services.controller.frontend``), so no dashboard is involved. While the operator has
reviews on, every closed exploration or rehearsal episode gets one review
(``services.behavior.analysis``):
- the operator record: ``<session>/operator-analysis/<episode_id>.json`` (0600), never
  mounted into the agent's container;
- the agent's copy: ``review.md`` in that episode's own published run directory (the
  ``artifacts.directory`` its ``finish`` or ``rehearse`` reply named), which the agent reads
  read-only under ``/workspace/runtime/autonomous_controller/runs/``. TASK.md says where.

Formal episodes are never reviewed. Gemini costs go to ``operator-analysis/usage.jsonl``
and never to the agent's own budget.

The session's episode management calls ``closed(episode_id)`` when an episode ends;

Layouts mirror ``omnigibson/eval/utils/eval_utils.py`` (ACTION_QPOS_INDICES and
PROPRIOCEPTION_INDICES for R1Pro) and ``omnigibson/eval/r1pro.yaml``. Only challenge-track
inputs are exposed: RGB, depth and the 61-D proprioception, plus odometry integrated from
the proprioceptive base velocity. No world pose, object state or segmentation.

symbols.name: action_layout

symbols.name: joint_limit_violations
symbols.doc: Describe absolute joints outside the actual bounds; do not alter measurements.

``diagnostics`` receives a bounded correction report for the public reply.
The input is never modified, including when a later row is rejected.

symbols.doc: Split the official 61-D proprioception into named fields.

symbols.doc:
Action row that keeps the base still and holds the measured arm/trunk joints.

``grippers`` is the last commanded (left, right) gripper value: the measured finger
opening is not a command, so holding repeats the previous command.

symbols.name: bounded_hold_action
symbols.doc:
Clamp an internally generated measured hold, regardless of excursion size.

Measurements remain raw. Explicit agent targets use validate_actions instead.
Finiteness and normalized command checks still apply to these generated rows.

symbols.doc:
Planar pose relative to the episode start, integrated from robot-frame base velocity.

Only the proprioceptive ``base_qvel`` ([vx, vy, wz] in the robot frame) is used, which
every challenge-track policy receives. Trapezoidal integration over one control period.

symbols.name: relative_goal
symbols.doc: Goal pose expressed in the odometry frame for a move relative to the current pose.

symbols.name: base_command
symbols.doc: Normalized base velocity toward ``goal`` (x, y, yaw) in the odometry frame.

summary:
BEHAVIOR-1K simulator process: one OmniGibson app, one task instance, one episode.

Runs only in ``runtime/envs/behavior``. The environment is constructed by the official
2026 ``BatchedEvaluator`` with the same configuration ``omnigibson.eval.eval`` builds
(partial scene load, human-demo-derived step limit, full-resolution RGB-D wrapper, fixed
evaluation seed), with a zero-action local policy because actions arrive over RPC.

symbols.name: preload_planner_libraries
symbols.doc:
Import the pinned warp and cuRobo before the Kit app starts: Isaac Sim bundles an older
omni.warp.core whose submodules would otherwise shadow warp-lang's and break cuRobo.

symbols.name: pin_render_gpu
symbols.doc:
Render on the simulator GPU. OmniGibson passes OMNIGIBSON_GPU_ID as both the CUDA
physics device and Kit's Vulkan renderer device; under CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES only the
former is remapped, so the renderer would land on physical GPU 0 and PhysX would find
no matching CUDA device. ROBODOJO_RENDER_GPU carries the physical index instead.

summary:
One BEHAVIOR-1K episode inside the OmniGibson process (runs in runtime/envs/behavior).

The official 2026 ``BatchedEvaluator`` (``num_envs=1``) owns environment creation, task
instance loading, settling, stepping and metrics, so this session reproduces the
organizers' evaluation exactly. The session adds the harness contract: identity-checked
RPC ops, challenge-track agent observations, start-relative odometry, and the trusted
operator files (``operator_state.json``, ``evaluation_outcome.json``, ``summary.json``,
``private_goal_report.json``)
that dashboards and formal scoring read. Nothing privileged is returned to the host
except inside those operator-only files.

symbols.name: _check_action_layout
symbols.doc: Fail fast if the robot's controller order differs from the published contract.

symbols.name: dof
symbols.doc: Robot joint indices driven by controller ``name`` (controllers are batched views).

symbols.name: _gripper_opening
symbols.doc:
Measured finger opening mapped onto [-1, 1] over the finger joint range, the
default output range of the smooth multi-finger gripper controller.

Runs after exploration closes, including after a bundle submission: both

episode. Every episode runs in its own worker process and child root.

symbols.name: resume_agent_formal
symbols.doc:
Finish an agent formal that was stopped before every layout had an outcome.

Episodes with an outcome stand. A stopped (interrupted) episode has none: its copy never
finished and it was never scored, so a fresh copy of the same frozen checkpoint plays that
layout from the start. The stopped attempt moves from the results to the batch's
interruptions record and its worker folder moves aside, so every reader of the results and
worker folders sees one episode per layout.

symbols.name: _worker_result

The worker's own episode record is authoritative.

A worker that started its episode but never finalized it counts as an error,
like a sequential timeout. One that never started an episode is a systemic
failure (spawn, preflight, bundle import), which interrupts the batch exactly
as it would in the sequential loop. A later nonzero worker exit is
recorded separately and cannot invalidate finalized task evidence.

Every layout is started at most once per run; a resumed agent formal skips the
episodes in ``done``, which already have an outcome. Gemini requests from all workers are
brokered here, so the session ledger and key stay in this process.
Episode numbers in batch state are 1-based, like formal_episode_index.

symbols.name: rendered_intrinsics

Match Isaac's square-pixel rendering, preserving horizontal FOV.

RoboDojo sets both apertures with maintain_square_pixels=False. The high
camera's vertical aperture disagrees with its image aspect ratio; Isaac's
intrinsics getter reads that stale value even though rendering uses square
pixels. For these unresized pinhole images, the effective fy is fx. Apply
this at native observation/preview publication, not to arbitrary user K
matrices in the general pixel-geometry utilities.

summary:
MCP stdio bridge for the native RoboDojo simulator.

The Isaac process remains the owner of simulation state.  This process owns the
MCP connection and talks to Isaac through RoboDojo's existing, lossless local
RPC.  It deliberately starts Isaac lazily, on the first automatic setup
request, so Codex can discover the tools without paying simulator startup cost.

The bridge implements the small MCP surface Codex needs directly with the
newline-delimited JSON-RPC stdio protocol.  That keeps the MCP server usable in
the pinned Isaac Python environment without installing another package into it.

Euler input is fixed-axis/extrinsic XYZ in radians. Axis-angle input is a
rotation vector whose norm is the angle. Matrix input is flat row-major and
must be orthonormal with determinant +1. Non-zero quaternion input is
normalized; all output is sign-standardized to a non-negative scalar part.

symbols.name: pose_math
symbols.doc:
Execute one validated, scene-independent high-level pose operation.

``compose_pose`` applies a local delta as ``T_base * T_delta``. An
environment delta adds translation directly in environment axes and
left-multiplies orientation as ``q_delta * q_base`` without rotating the
base position about the environment origin. ``relative_pose`` is the exact
inverse under the selected convention. ``format_target`` and
``extract_target`` translate between general poses and the named RoboDojo
EEF/cuRobo target fields without reading or advancing simulation.

summary:

Sources are markdown with Jinja statements on their own lines, e.g.

    {% if camera_geometry %}
    ...text for depth-capable profiles...
    {% else %}
    ...RGB-only text...
    {% endif %}

trim_blocks/lstrip_blocks drop the statement lines entirely, so rendered text keeps
the source's line layout. Unknown names fail the build (StrictUndefined).

{{ block("<id>") }} on a line of its own; the setup's facts, the recipe's `vocab`
and any keyword parameters are available inside a block. Every block a file uses
is recorded, so a build can report which blocks produced each file.

account signs in once in its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR and issues a long-lived

(login.Credential):

      claude-experiment.token            the token (0600), read at each launch
      claude-experiment.json             identity (0600): email, organization, created_at

from a session's next launch.

- a detailed operator-side review (Gemini, the session's review ledger) from the simulator's

Reviews of finished BEHAVIOR exploration episodes from the simulator's ground truth.

Operator-side, stdlib + numpy only. The simulator writes ``sim/private_goal_report.json``
(every grounded goal condition with its initial and final truth, and the extents of the
objects involved). This module classifies the conditions, describes each missed one in
relative geometry, and asks Gemini for a short explanation using that report, the
episode's tool trace and its final frames.

Two outputs: the full operator record (report, explanation, cost), and the agent-facing
review. A standard review is the analyst's explanation alone and carries no scores. A
detailed review adds the episode's partial score and the ground-truth goal checklist with
its geometry, and the analyst may quote exact numbers. Either names objects only by their
task names (``detergent bottle 1``) and carries no scene names or world coordinates.
Formal episodes are never reviewed live; a finished code-mode session's runs of its own code
are reviewed for its later live copies (``services/agent_formal/code_runs.py``), from the
code's log as well.

summary:
cuRobo free-space arm planning inside the OmniGibson process (runs in runtime/envs/behavior).

Challenge-compliant: the planner's world collision checker is created empty and never
updated (``skip_obstacle_update=True``), so it avoids self-collision only and never reads
scene meshes. Targets arrive in the robot base frame (the frame of the proprioceptive EEF
poses). The wrapper plans relative to the holonomic base's virtual root link and refreshes
the locked joints (virtual base, and the trunk for ``arm_no_torso``) from the current state,
so targets are converted to world coordinates here, inside the simulator; the world pose
never leaves this process. Plans become native 23-D rows at the control rate and run
through the ordinary episode step path.

symbols.name: generator
symbols.doc:
cuRobo's ARM embodiment (trunk and both arms) or its arms-only variant (trunk locked
at its current joints by the wrapper's per-plan locked-joint refresh).

On sm_120 GPUs the arms-only variant's finetune trajopt would launch cuRobo's fused
L-BFGS kernel (history 27) with 392 threads x 168 registers, over the per-block
register limit ("too many resources requested for launch"; NVlabs/curobo#716). The
trunk-enabled variant already uses cuRobo's PyTorch L-BFGS step there, so the
arms-only finetune solver is configured the same way.

trunk, base and other arm hold their measured joints. Uses the robot's relative
Jacobian (base-body frame) each control step. Local and not collision-aware, like
RoboDojo's EEF stepping.
